#9846. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

InfoQ Homepage News Uno Platform 7.0 Adds WebGPU Backend, Apple TV and Reactor Support, and Retires Native Rendering

Nov 16, 2026 3 min read

The Uno Platform team released Uno Platform 7.0, which unifies rendering on SkiaSharp 4 with an experimental WebGPU backend, adds Apple TV as a target platform and supports .NET 11 from day zero. The release also brings third-party .NET MAUI controls and Microsoft.UI.Reactor library to every target, and removes native rendering and Mac Catalyst.

Uno Platform is an open-source framework for building .NET applications with C# and WinUI XAML for Windows, Android, iOS, macOS, Linux and WebAssembly. The team describes 7.0 as its largest release, with 5,219 commits and 704 closed issues since 6.7. According to the team’s benchmarks, 7.0 is about 2x faster at the median and 5x smaller than 6.7, with some operations, such as brush creation, up to 38x faster. These figures come from the vendor and the workloads were not published in detail.

All targets now render through one pluggable pipeline. SkiaSharp 4 is the default, and Uno Platform is a co-maintainer of the library alongside the .NET team at Microsoft. On Android, Windows and Linux, Skia now renders through Vulkan by default. The WebGPU backend, available on all desktop, mobile and WebAssembly targets, is enabled by adding WebGpu to UnoFeatures and registering the backend on the host builder. It uses wgpu-native outside the browser and the browser’s own WebGPU support on WebAssembly. The team measured up to a 50% frame-rate improvement depending on the scene, and says a WebGPU-only app drops about 6 MB of uncompressed native code from WebAssembly builds. A new WebGpuCanvasElement lets applications issue their own WebGPU commands inside the UI.

Through .NET MAUI Embedding, controls from vendors such as Syncfusion, Telerik, Infragistics, DevExpress and Esri previously ran only on iOS, Android, macOS and Windows. They now work on every Uno Platform target, including the web and Linux. In the other direction, existing .NET MAUI apps can reach the browser and Linux through Uno Platform’s .NET MAUI handlers.

Microsoft.UI.Reactor, Microsoft’s declarative C# framework for WinUI with hooks such as UseState and no XAML, now runs on desktop, browser, Android and iOS. It is enabled with the Reactor UnoFeature, is in preview, and can coexist with existing XAML pages in the same visual tree. Apple TV support is added through the net10.0-tvos target framework, targets tvOS 15 and later, renders through Metal and uses the Siri Remote for focus navigation. .NET 11 is supported on every head, for example through dotnet new unoapp -tfm net11.0, while .NET 10 remains the long-term support option.

RichTextBlock and RichEditBox are now available on every platform, closing an issue opened in 2018. WinUI alignment continues with ItemsRepeater and ItemsView ported from current WinUI sources, LinedFlowLayout, the TitleBar control, multiple windows on iPad and Lottie rendering through Composition. Smaller additions include built-in input validation through INotifyDataErrorInfo, TalkBack, VoiceOver and AT-SPI screen-reader support, and the uno-devserver app command for launching and inspecting running apps from scripts and CI.

Most apps upgrade by changing the Uno.Sdk version in global.json, following the migration guide. The team released Uno Platform Studio 3.3 alongside it.

The release follows Uno Platform 6.7 in September, which added Android TV, Android Auto and Wear OS targets, semantic styles shared by the Material and Simple themes, and damage-region repainting on Skia renderers. It also removed the WPF targets.

#9844. Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

A operação, que contou com o uso de inteligência artificial, utilizou e-mails falsos, documentos governamentais falsificados e a criação de uma organização local para atacar escolas no Peru e no Equador, entre outras ações.

This translation was generated with our internal AI tool.

Uma operação de influência sediada na Rússia enviou e-mails se passando por autoridades educacionais do Peru e do Equador, levando algumas escolas a realizar eventos que os operadores então utilizaram para alimentar controvérsias, de acordo com um relatório divulgado pela OpenAI.

A operação de “fachada falsa”, apelidada de “Dark Clark,” utilizou uma combinação de planejamento baseado em IA e relatórios, além de técnicas mais tradicionais, para convencer administradores escolares a celebrar um “Dia Nacional da Diversidade Cultural e Linguística” em 21 de maio e a destacar três figuras políticas ucranianas, que foram então usadas para tentar semear divisão, afirmou a OpenAI em uma análise do uso operacional de seus modelos de IA. Em outras campanhas, como as direcionadas à Argentina e à Bolívia, as operações russas pareciam ter como objetivo influenciar a política local.

Related:China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

Os supostos operadores russos utilizaram IA para tornar seu fluxo de trabalho mais eficiente, redigindo relatórios internos sobre suas atividades e, em alguns casos, criando conteúdo para suas campanhas, informou a empresa.

“A IA pode conferir a essas operações de fachada maior escala, eficiência, fluência linguística e capacidade editorial”, afirmou a OpenAI em sua análise. “Os operadores podem usar essas vantagens para explorar vítimas desavisadas, como funcionários ou editores, e divulgar seu conteúdo para públicos que não têm ideia de quem está por trás disso, nem quais são suas motivações.”

A América Latina tornou-se um palco cibernético de espionagem e operações de influência na disputa entre as principais potências globais, tornando-se a região mais atacada ciberneticamente no mundo. Atores conhecidos ligados à China tiveram como alvo tanto a Venezuela quanto o Panamá no início deste ano para obter informações sobre a política na região e proteger os interesses petrolíferos do país. A Rússia expandiu suas operações de inteligência cibernética e desinformação, principalmente para frustrar os esforços dos EUA na região, de acordo com um relatório da RAND de 2026.

“A Rússia também mantém capacidades cibernéticas para realizar invasões direcionadas e desinformação com o objetivo de semear divisão política, perturbar a percepção da situação e enfraquecer as mensagens dos EUA em situações de crise”, afirmou o relatório da RAND.

A operação russa parece estar ligada a uma entidade conhecida como “Politology” ou “La Compania”, que tem vínculos com o falecido oligarca russo Yevgeniy Prigozhin, com o objetivo de influenciar a política global, de acordo com a análise da OpenAI. Os relatórios fornecidos ao modelo de IA continham informações detalhadas sobre as operações do grupo, incluindo detalhes sobre trabalhos anteriores que os ligavam aos grupos de Prigozhin.

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

O ataque de desinformação contra escolas em Lima, no Peru, foi uma das campanhas descritas pelos atacantes. Ao elaborar uma diretiva com aparência oficial para os administradores escolares, citando um fictício “Dia da Diversidade Cultural e Linguística”, eles solicitaram que os alunos participassem de atividades de 10 a 15 minutos para aprender sobre três figuras políticas ucranianas. Posteriormente, os operadores instruíram os administradores a enviar fotos do evento.

A OpenAI investigou os eventos e encontrou detalhes que corroboravam as alegações dos operadores, disse Ben Nimmo, pesquisador-chefe da equipe de inteligência e investigações da OpenAI, à Dark Reading. O Ministério da Educação do Peru emitiu uma carta oficial (em espanhol) dois meses depois, mencionando a diretiva e informando que a embaixada da Ucrânia havia identificado a fraude em sua própria carta, datada de 25 de maio.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

“Nunca se deve acreditar em um agente de ameaças pelo que ele diz, certo?”, diz Nimmo. “ Para cada alegação, buscamos evidências na internet que a corroborassem. Para algumas das alegações que eles fizeram, simplesmente não conseguimos encontrar evidências. Talvez tenham sido removidas, talvez estivessem em lugares que não seriam encontrados por meio de uma busca em fontes abertas, talvez nunca tenham acontecido.”

Uma diretiva fraudulenta enviada às escolas de Lima, no Peru, por supostos agentes de desinformação russos. Fonte: Ministério da Educação do Peru (traduzido pelo Claude Opus 5.5)

Como a operação resultou em um político na Polônia citando os eventos, a OpenAI classificou o sucesso com nota 5 na Escala de Impacto de Operações de Influência de seis pontos.

Os operadores russos usaram técnicas semelhantes para induzir escolas no Equador a realizar uma cerimônia de juramento de lealdade ao presidente Daniel Noboa e a Erik Prince, ex-chefe da empresa militar privada Blackwater, afirmou a OpenAI em sua análise. Algumas escolas seguiram a orientação, o que levou a cobertura jornalística e uma denúncia oficial por parte do Ministro da Educação.

Os operadores alegaram ter conduzido com sucesso outras operações de influência das quais a OpenAI não conseguiu encontrar evidências, incluindo a divulgação de uma história de que uma influenciadora brasileira nas redes sociais teria sido traficada para a Ucrânia e a disseminação de um trecho de áudio que alegava que bancos bolivianos pretendiam limitar saques em dinheiro. Os operadores também, ocasionalmente, pediam ao ChatGPT para encontrar incidentes regionais pelos quais pudessem assumir o crédito, diz Nimmo.

Os operadores russos criaram uma chamada “plataforma de pesquisa”, denominada Social Research Center, que contratava funcionários regionais para criar conteúdo local, sem que eles soubessem que a organização fazia parte de uma iniciativa de desinformação.

Embora as operações tivessem como alvo a América Latina, a intenção era prejudicar as relações entre a Ucrânia e o resto do mundo, afirma Nimmo, da OpenAI.

“A maneira como eu encaro essa operação como um todo é que ela gira em torno da Ucrânia”, diz ele. “Trata-se de fazer a Ucrânia parecer mal.”

De modo geral, o uso da IA não abriu novos caminhos para ataques nem criou novas oportunidades de desinformação, mas a tecnologia fez com que as traduções para o idioma nativo soassem mais naturais, permitiu que os operadores assumissem papéis específicos com mais facilidade e simplificou o fluxo de trabalho da operação, afirma Nimmo.

“Se você pensar na Agência de Pesquisa na Internet e no inglês desleixado deles, acho que a IA realmente oferece uma vantagem incremental”, diz ele. “Mas não tenho a impressão de que o uso do nosso modelo tenha sido o fator decisivo. De certa forma, o manual de táticas era muito, muito tradicional.”

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9843. Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

#9842. Paint in the memory of other programs

core is a program that I wrote which spills the viscera of other programs onto the screen and allows you to prod them. it could be called an “esoteric debugger” or a “paint program.”

the visual content of the program is constructed as follows:

as well as the display of program memory, core allows for its manipulation. if core shows you a picture of a program’s insides, then it is only natural that it allows you to scribble on it. the overcommitted empty space below the stack stack provides an inviting empty space to scribble in. it’s a perfect place to hide your terrible secrets in some poor, innocent process.

core is the logical conclusion of blinkenlights, “Allblinkenlights,” if you will. the intended experience is evocative aimlessness. the human visual system is highly parallel and very good at recognizing patterns. you are encouraged to allow these patterns to wash over you.

many textures arise from different kinds of data in memory. ASCII text is incredibly recognizable, by virtue of being a 7-bit encoding, as well as having a biased distribution of values. 64-bit pointers are similarly easy to recognize because their last two bytes will either be zero or one.

in the mesmerizing undulations of complex programs, these textures may blink or move around or stay boringly still. if you are keen, you may catch some large data structure being allocated or filled in. or you may see the first generation of a garbage collector fly by as short-lived objects are created at a rapid rate. in games, the stack can be seen flickering rapidly and changing every frame.

core can make stark the immensity of memory and the way that programs use it. data structures and programming patterns appear in the physical reality of which bits are toggled where.

I was very keen to see what a program would look like that uses continuation passing style implemented as in the famous paper, CONS should not CONS its arguments, part II: Cheney on the M.T.A. I compiled a game programmed in CHICKEN scheme and was delighted to see a stack that moved like a waterfall.

graphical programs can be the most interesting. visual patterns in graphics in memory can emerge vividly.

when attached to virtual machines or emulators, core gains omniscience over an entire operating system.

it is astounding to see an immense creature flicker to life. pages fill empty space in speckled patterns. panning over a chasm, the page tables can be seen vibrating and filling in with new allocations. it is reminiscent, perhaps, of insects, like a beehive.

one could not hope to wholly understand the way that physical memory is arranged, but they may peer voyeuristically into random pages of process memory, abound with text strings and recognizable graphics.

programs often exist in the mind as something ineffable, intangible, and abstract. even their physical existence is locked inside black plastic squares, harboring impossibly tiny transistors. in my opinion, to lay visceral the individual bits in a computer program is an idea that despite being simple, is immensely potent.

#9841. UK Warns Its Critical Infrastructure Faces Grave Risk

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Britain's new Labour-led government is making a concerted push to get ahead of the AI risks to its national networks and the industrial complex.

At various levels of the United Kingdom government, officials are warning about the threat of cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure.

His Majesty's Government broadcast its cybersecurity agenda on Nov. 3, releasing a variety of policy papers, an annual report from its lead cybersecurity agency, and related announcements pertaining to the security of small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs), supply chain vendors, critical national infrastructure (CNI), and more. These items all followed from an updated Autumn Budget 2026, released last week, which provisioned nearly two hundred billion pounds for AI-driven government cybersecurity projects.

Amid all of the practical policy updates, the headline quote of the day came from the state's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which assessed that it's "highly likely that between now and 2028, AI‑powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI." It also labeled "highly likely" the prospect that "China, Russia, and other nation states will routinely use AI cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals" in the country.

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

In a new report, Manchester-based NCC Group polled Members of Parliament (MPs) about the state of the UK's CNI cybersecurity posture. About half (51%) of MPs reported that their areas of the country are "not keeping pace" with the threats to its infrastructure. Only 22% expressed confidence in their country's posture. Asked about the nation's ability to fight off a major attack against its CNI, 47% believe that it's unprepared, whereas 41% feel it is.

The survey data is best read as aspirational, not prescriptive. There's little evidence that the UK is less prepared than other nations in addressing threats to its critical infrastructure, or that politicians would be able to tell one way or the other. Leaders are simply aware of the magnitude of what faces them.

"The challenge isn't a lack of government action; it's proof that action translates into resilience," says Katharina Sommer, head of government affairs at NCC Group. "There's still no tested blueprint for coordinating cyber response effectively across government and industry, and that’s not a problem unique to the UK. The test for critical infrastructure operators is whether they can demonstrate, before an attack hits, that they can sustain essential services, recover quickly and maintain public confidence," which remains an open question.

A clearer message came through on Nov. 3, from the experts at the NCSC. Using a scale in which "likely" accords with roughly 55% to 75% odds, "highly likely" with 80% to 90% odds, and "almost certain" approaching 100%, it bet that it is:

Related:AIを活用したサイバー攻撃の増加を受け、日本がサイバーセキュリティへの緊急資金拠出を推進

Likely that threat actors will use AI cyber tools to needle vulnerabilities in CNI

Highly likely that nation-states will use AI to increase the speed and sophistication of their cyberattacks, in service of their geopolitical goals in the UK; in particular, the agency identified China as the foremost player in terms of intent and capability to hit CNI and other strategic targets

Almost certain that "many systems will remain vulnerable" to AI-empowered attacks

The NCSC also drew out some future scenarios. Optimistically, it acknowledged that AI-driven cyber threat development might slow, allowing a window of time for the UK to catch up with the problem. Pessimistically, it painted a picture in which AI threats totally outpace the UK's ability to keep up.

"The situation is likely to be worse than is currently known, with many variables and unknowns still to be discovered," according to the report.

The message out of the UK government on Tuesday was, more or less: we're trying to get ahead of this.

In a policy paper, the government acknowledged that 2018's Network and Information Systems (NIS) Regulations — the UK's only multisector cybersecurity law — is "out of date and insufficient to tackle the threats we face." In a speech announcing its Annual Review 2026, NCSC CEO Richard Horne called the law built to replace NIS 2018 — November 2025's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill — "a vital step forward." The updated bill brings data centers, managed service providers (MSPs), and specific "critical suppliers" into the fold, and introduces stricter breach reporting requirements and hefty fines for negligence.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

In a separate policy paper concerning the same bill, the government stated its intention to introduce a new vendor risk management framework focused specifically on the "national security risks posed by vendors" connected to essential service providers. And in yet a third, related paper, the government described how the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will be used to account for agentic "loss of control" incidents, in the fashion of this summer's AI industry lab leaks. Projected future measures include:

Security and resilience requirements to prevent loss of control incidents

Empowering ministers to perform postmortems

The bill is currently passing through Parliament.

Besides this one bill, the UK government also announced £2.4 billion in subsidies to help micro-, small, and medium-sized businesses attain "Cyber Essentials" certifications. All of this week's announcements come on the heels of an Autumn Budget last week, which arranged for tens of billions of pounds each to fund, among other things:

A National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, for vulnerability discovery across the country, including CNI

A National Cyber Shield, for training AI agents to automate cyber defense

A separate National Agentic Security Unit for fighting rogue AI agents

"Increasing the funding and focus on cybersecurity to help keep the UK secure is very welcome," says Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence for KnowBe4. At the same time, he adds, "the main challenge I see is scale."

"£154 million for cyber-defenses is a good step," he believes, "but the NCSC estimates cyberattacks cost UK organizations £14.7 billion a year."

Dark Reading asked cybersecurity experts what governments like the UK's need to do to prevent future worst-case scenarios. They consistently emphasized the same point:

"AI did not create new weaknesses; it revealed them. Most incidents still start through the same familiar routes, such as phishing, stolen credentials, and the traditional kill chain paths attackers have relied on for years. The key to stopping these threats is, surprisingly, not exciting: it's the fundamentals," Chapman argues.

The fundamentals for Graham Taylor CBE, director of defense strategy for Northern Europe at OPSWAT, start with protecting the edge. "Too many critical sites rely on firewalls and VPNs for connections that only need to send data one way. Where a facility only exports monitoring data, a hardware-enforced data diode removes the return path entirely, so neither a human attacker nor AI can use that link to send commands into the facility," he says.

Jacob Krell, Suzu Labs senior director for secure AI solutions and cybersecurity, emphasizes network segmentation "built like a boat." AI is going to make the perimeter easier to breach, he says, "and it cuts the time to objective once an attacker is inside. Critical infrastructure is notoriously vulnerable here because operators are hesitant to patch and test systems, and their caution is rational; a bad update takes a plant offline. So the perimeter fails more often and the interior offers nothing to slow lateral movement."

John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, tosses out a less conventional suggestion for fighting off AI threats to CNI. "If AI gives attackers the ability to do a tremendous amount of work very quickly, defenders have an opportunity to present them with large numbers of decoys to investigate," he says. "We need creative ways to make those decoys look realistic and dynamic. The more time attacking AI agents spend interacting with decoys, the less time they spend attacking real systems."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

Version 0.46 of the Zellij terminal workspace has been released.

This release includes a major addition in Zellij: Zellij is now also a desktop terminal. To run it: zellij terminal. It works on linux, mac and windows.

Nothing changes for the normal multiplexer - Zellij can still run inside another terminal. Both sessions are the same and can be shared.

#9839. Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Europe's supermarket freezer hacks show how security issues can cascade across an industry, disrupting supply chains at scale.

The recent refrigerator hacks wreaking havoc across European supermarkets is a lesson in how shared weaknesses in operational technology (OT) can spread across a whole supply chain.

On the night of Oct. 11, an attacker reportedly compromised refrigeration controls used by hundreds of French supermarkets, triggering extended defrost cycles in refrigerators and freezers across the country. The incident caused millions of euros in damage across roughly 700 affected stores in France alone, spoiling food, damaging equipment, and even reportedly starting some fires in the process.

The technology leveraged in these attacks included Danfoss refrigeration controllers, as well as Dixell and Copeland XWEB systems. It's unclear how the threat actor gained access to these systems.

However, the Danfoss controllers at the center of this campaign ran Internet-accessible Web servers. Many were accessible using default login credentials: "admin" as the username and the current date as the password. CERT-FR made a number of recommendations in an advisory to affected supermarkets, such as changing default passwords, factory resetting compromised equipment, and updating firmware. Though to that last point, Danfoss told AFP that many of the attacks involved legacy products that no longer receive updates.

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

France's Cyber Crisis Coordination Center (C4) on Nov. 9 published a five page report attributing the series of attacks on Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and specifically on the IRGC's Shahid Shoostari and Shahid Kaveh cyber-offensive units.

France's Ministry of Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement that the country will propose to its European partners new sanctions against the Iranian entities and individuals allegedly involved in the cyberattack, adding that France reserves the right to take additional proportionate measures to respond to the attacks.

What stands out about the French supermarket attacks is how a shared weakness in refrigeration infrastructure appears to have enabled disruption across hundreds of stores. While investigators have not publicly confirmed the initial access vector, the incident raises questions about the risks created when organizations rely on similar technologies, deployment models, and remote-access practices.

Chris St. Myers, director of SentinelLABS, says evidence suggests a common exposure problem, rather than market concentration, may have facilitated this issue.

"CERT-FR confirmed that the French compromises involved Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, along with Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems. These technologies are deployed across many retail environments, often with similar remote access requirements and configurations," St. Meyers says. "That creates opportunities for attackers to reuse the same techniques across otherwise unrelated organizations."

Related:EU Grocers Pay a Steep Price for Unpatched Fridge Firmware

Thomas Plank, CEO of industrial security firm Tributech, similarly diagnosed common exposure as a core issue behind the attacks.

"What's concentrated is the setup. Across chains and countries, it's the same model: remote-management controllers reachable from the internet, often on out-of-support firmware, maintained by a small number of contractors who look after hundreds of stores from one place," Plank tells Dark Reading. "When everyone runs the same risky pattern through the same few channels, one way in reaches many retailers at once, across borders, overnight. That's why this looks like a campaign rather than a string of unlucky stores."

It's highly unusual and hardly precedented for a cyberattack to have such a significant impact on the food supply chain, but it's not the only incident like it in recent memory.

A similar attack hit refrigeration and freezer systems in stores across other countries at the beginning of November, including Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden. Around the same time, attackers targeted the refrigeration of three blood banks operated by the national French Blood Establishment, though the attack was stopped before blood plasma was damaged.

Related:How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

For as alarming and impactful these incidents may seem, supply chain targeting has become more common in recent years with 2021's Colonial Pipeline attack, Iran's recent targeting of fuel monitoring systems around the US, and 2024's Change Healthcare incident.

The danger is clear, especially in the context of a supermarket. Piotr Buliński, chief technology officer (CTO) of Internet of Things (IoT) device management firm Qbee, says a supermarket chain runs thousands of small, unattended OT systems between refrigeration, HVAC, and building management. "Each one is 'just a few controllers,' so nobody treats them as critical infrastructure," he says. "Yet when they fail, the damage is immediate and physical."

These incidents remind us once again about the importance of securing critical infrastructure.

Updating OT systems is a challenging task in their own right because of the downtime often required. Much of the critical technology holding up industrial processes is intended to operate for years (if not decades) on end, while the organizations relying on OT can often include those too under-resourced to have dedicated security staff, like municipalities, or indeed, supermarkets.

Even as these problems have gotten a little easier to address over the years and many dedicated firms have risen to address these challenges, organizations still struggle to secure OT.

St. Meyers believes retail OT has historically received less security attention than traditional industrial environments, despite carrying many of the same underlying risks. He says this is possibly in part because refrigeration, HVAC, and building management systems are "often deployed and maintained outside the traditional IT security organization," despite being OT.

Plank agrees. He says one solution for retailers is to verify commands at the device level against engineering limits, as "no freezer should ever accept a command to go to 50°C, whoever sends it and whatever channel it arrives on," referencing the extreme temperatures some targeted equipment reached during the attacks.

For organizations outside the sphere of influence that want to learn from what happened here, there are several lessons: Don't use default passwords, take inventory of where and how industrial technologies are internet accessible, remove internet exposure wherever possible, and make sure all points of access are secured.

Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat research at Sophos, tells Dark Reading that generally, this incident should be seen as a warning to retailers. "Industrial systems, from energy production to water management to food refrigeration, must be secured," he says, "and at a minimum not accessible to malicious hackers via the Internet."

This story was updated at 2:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 9 to reflect France's accusations against Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

#9838. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

#9836. AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

Security records are increasingly being used by vendors to train their models, creating new risks for enterprises.

Traditionally, security incident records have served a singular, very important purpose: to document what the organization observed, decided, and did. Closure notes, rule text, false-positive dispositions, and the reason why an alert was dropped are treated by security teams as records contained in the ticket queue. For organizations to reconstruct their decisions and, crucially, be accountable for them later, all of this evidence must be retained.

To be sure, security automation is anything but new. For years, SOAR platforms have executed playbooks, closed alerts, and recorded dispositions. They run a rule that customers wrote. The change is what happens to the record afterward, as a portion of the evidence has an alternate destination for a different purpose. Once incident records are ingested into a security AI system with permission to capture data for model building or validation, this evidence can become data the vendor uses for model development and validation.

Related:AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

A sufficiently large collection of prompts and related records can offer more than a glimpse into which signals are treated by the organization as meaningful, which detections are suppressed, what analysts mark as benign, and where it misses something.

A single closure is a comparatively harmless note. A series, however, presents a map; suppressing the same class of alerts delineates boundaries of concern. The rationales for closures indicate acceptable levels of PowerShell noise or failed logins that warrant a ticket. Tuning decisions encode which signals the team stops trusting and when. The contents of the ticket do not need to be accessed by an external party for it to understand the pattern, which is the sensitive portion.

This isn't about reconstructing an AI incident; that's a logging decision. Nor is it about prompt injection, or the familiar case of a vendor training on customer chat logs. The problem is what happens when ordinary security records acquire a second use.

Microsoft Security Copilot provides an option for the owner to allow Microsoft to capture and human-review Security Copilot data to enhance and validate Microsoft's security-specific model, which is built on the Azure OpenAI foundation model. The data captured for model improvement can include whatever Microsoft plug-ins and Security Copilot agents have used while interacting with the product. The documentation states that this data is not used to train the foundation model and is not shared with OpenAI. A second setting controls the capture of data for the purpose of product-performance reviews.

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

The default for each setting depends on the method of provisioning the workspace. With the exception of Microsoft 365 E5 and E7 auto-provisioning, data sharing is enabled by default. The customer that enabled the setting has made an intentional decision, but the customer that has not viewed the settings page may not know which default applies. Using the service and allowing a vendor to capture data for model development or validation are different decisions, and Microsoft has already made them separable.

The archive had one job: namely, to help the organization reconstruct and defend its own decisions. Now the same records may be held by a vendor for model development or validation, which in turn creates new risks. A vendor breach puts the records outside the customer's network, while a legal demand can expose them without the customer's control. The retention rules and access controls were built for an archive the organization controlled, but they were not built for a second copy elsewhere.

An auditable record has to preserve more than the final decision. It has to distinguish what the organization knew, what the analyst decided, what the system was given, and what the system recommended. Otherwise, the model's observation effectively becomes the decision. Counsel asking what the organization knew at the time of the incident will not be satisfied by this. An auditor asking why the detections were tuned down should not be met with the closure rationale that also appears in the evidence stream.

Related:People Are Getting Weird About AI

This belongs in the procurement contract. A vendor's use of customer security records to provide a service does not by itself authorize their use for model improvement, and evidence retention and model development are different things that should require separate permission. Rule content, closure notes, and ticket text should not be covered by a generic AI clause. If the vendor wants the data for model improvement, then this should be an explicit, revocable choice.

Until these uses are formally separated, the archive has two functions. One of them continues, as expected, to be operated by the organization. The other turns all the evidence into the vendor's resource.

Gerald Mako has more than a decade of experience advising European and Asian governments on artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and technology strategy. His work focuses on AI governance, cyber resilience, and the security challenges created by increasingly autonomous systems.

Chief Information Security Officer, Cobham Satcom

Lemuel Valdez has led cybersecurity and security transformation across private equity portfolios, government, and critical infrastructure environments. He has advised and supported more than 20 PE-backed companies on cyber risk, due diligence, incident response, security architecture, and regulatory compliance.

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field

Nov 16, 2026 4 min read

AWS has launched Nitro Sandboxes, which run an opted-in Kubernetes pod, ECS task, or EC2 workload inside its own lightweight virtual machine with a separate guest kernel, carved out of a running EC2 instance by the Nitro hypervisor. On Amazon EKS, the whole change is one pod field: runtimeClassName: isolated-sandbox or confidential-sandbox.

The feature is available in all commercial regions at no additional charge, and AWS positions it for workloads where the tenant or the code cannot be trusted, with coding agents named first. In an AWS blog post, Carlos Santana and Trishi Mehta write:

Each pod gets its own operating system, completely separate from the host and from every neighbor.

According to the EKS documentation, a containerd-shim-nitro-sandbox-v2 process on the parent instance launches a Firecracker microVM as a first-level guest with hardware-assisted virtualization, after which an agent inside the VM runs the pod’s containers through its own containerd and the two sides communicate over virtio and vsock. The result is a sandbox that shares neither kernel nor memory mappings with the parent instance or any other sandbox, while the containers themselves start unchanged. How the nodes get there depends on the cluster type: on EKS Auto Mode the two RuntimeClasses ship with every cluster and sandbox-capable nodes are provisioned on demand, whereas on standard EKS a team builds a sandbox-enabled AMI for its node groups or Karpenter.

What separates the two modes is which side of the boundary is trusted. Isolated mode trusts the parent instance and not the guest, which is why kubectl exec, logs, and process listing keep working, whereas confidential mode treats the parent as untrusted and moves enforcement inside the VM: a Cedar policy generated from the pod spec pins image digests, arguments, environment, mounts and capabilities, exec and stdin are denied, the Nitro Secure Module measures the image and policy into PCRs, and a KMS key policy can release secrets only to a sandbox whose measurements match. Image layers can be encrypted as well, so the parent moves ciphertext it never reads.

That chain only holds if something checks the measurements, and the documentation says so: without a KMS policy or external verifier checking the PCR values, "the attestation measurement is recorded but never verified, and the confidentiality guarantees of confidential mode are incomplete." Separately from either mode, a network-isolated annotation boots the sandbox with no network device at all, which also removes DNS, NTP, IMDS and Pod Identity and breaks HTTP and TCP probes.

Sandip Das, an AWS Container Hero, read the documentation the same way and drew out what isolated mode leaves to the operator: the protection "only runs in one direction," so a compromised parent can still observe or tamper with unencrypted traffic and DNS, writes the pod's /etc/hosts, and can mint Pod Identity credentials for any pod on the node. He also lists prerequisites the blog post does not, among them Kubernetes 1.36 or later, a launch template with Nitro Enclaves enabled on managed node groups, without which "sandboxed pods sit in Pending," and Pod Identity rather than IRSA for credentials. On AWS's description of performance as near-native, he advises treating it "as a vendor claim" and benchmarking startup latency, I/O throughput and tail latency.

Beyond agents, AWS lists multi-tenant SaaS, regulated workloads, CI builds and remote IDEs, and points to the open-source agent-sandbox project for warm pools that hand out a pre-booted VM in about two seconds.

The constraints are on the considerations page, and the largest is GPU and device passthrough, which is not supported at launch because Firecracker cannot pass host devices into a guest, so GPU pods run without the sandbox class. Density is capped twice over: total sandbox vCPUs may not exceed five times the node's vCPU count, and neither may the number of sandboxes, halved on CPU-overcommit types, which gives a 4-vCPU node room for twenty 1-vCPU sandboxes or five 4-vCPU ones. Simultaneous multithreading costs more than the arithmetic suggests, because core scheduling stops two sandboxes sharing the sibling threads of one core and leaves roughly half the advertised vCPUs usable; Graviton, with one thread per core, is unaffected.

The nearest comparison is GKE Sandbox, which has offered a gvisor RuntimeClass since 2019 and more recently a microvm class built on Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor. gVisor intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel, starts in under 200 milliseconds and supports CUDA on a subset of GPUs; Google's microVM option carries a fixed 250 mCPU and 130 MiB per pod, starts in one to two seconds and does not support GPUs. AWS has taken the VM side of that split and expressed its overhead as density and threads rather than per-pod resources.

On EC2, Amazon Linux and Firecracker are supported natively and patches are available for other virtual machine monitors. The EC2 User Guide carries the supported instance list and notes that snapshot, restore and live migration are not available.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

#9833. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

#9832. Enabling the parallel frontend on nightly

TL;DR: We are enabling the parallel frontend of the Rust compiler on nightly by default, to find remaining issues in preparation for its stabilization.

The Rust compiler has been using multiple threads to compile code in its "backend" part (using LLVM) for a long time. However, its "frontend" part (which includes type checking and borrow checking) has been executing sequentially, on a single thread, which of course limits the performance of the compiler. If you are interested in a more in-depth explanation of parallelism in the Rust compiler, see this previous post.

The compiler frontend actually had support for running in parallel for a long time, but it was not enabled by default due to various issues. Three years ago, we made it possible to opt into the parallel frontend on the nightly channel, with the plan to stabilize it in 2024. Clearly, we did not achieve that goal, but work on the parallel frontend was still slowly progressing in the meantime.

Last year, Vadim Petrochenkov, together with several other contributors, started a coordinated effort to finally get the parallel frontend over the finish line. Since then, many long-standing issues were fixed, and its performance was improved. Now we are at a point where we would like to make it widely available. But before that, we want to find out if people encounter issues with it in the wild, which is why we are enabling it by default only on the nightly channel. Once we will be confident enough that it is working well, we want to stabilize it.

The parallel frontend has been enabled on the nightly channel by default since nightly-2026-11-14.

The primary benefit of enabling the parallel frontend is, of course, faster compilation of Rust programs.

We benchmarked the parallel frontend in our benchmark suite, which measures the duration to compile the leaf crate in a crate graph. As usual, the results were varied. In some benchmarks, the parallel frontend barely helped. In others, for example when performing a cargo check of the nalgebra, cargo or diesel crates, the compilation was almost three times faster, using 8 threads.

In the table below, you can find the aggregated wall-time mean change for the real-world benchmarks in our suite, when building a single crate from scratch across several configurations, compared to the same build using a sequential frontend.

It is clear that the parallelization is not perfect, and we definitely plan to invest more effort into improving its performance. Nevertheless, with 8 threads, it can make the end-to-end compilation time of cargo check ~2x faster for several crates that we tested, which is still quite an improvement.

The performance benefits for incremental rebuilds are much more modest, and also very hard to compare, because the performance of rebuilds depends on what was changed and how were the codegen units laid out. In our benchmark suite, we saw a mean improvement of 3-5% for incremental rebuilds. But we currently do not have great benchmarks for this use-case, so your results might vary.

We can also zoom in on an individual crate. Here is a chart of how the wall-time scales when compiling the nalgebra 0.33 crate, for a full non-incremental build (full), full incremental build (incr-full) and an incremental rebuild (incr-patched) across several build configurations:

What is interesting to note is that enabling the parallel frontend can actually also make the backend faster, for reasons explained here.

It is important to note that all benchmark results presented above measured only the compilation of a single crate. When compiling a whole crate graph, your CPU cores might already be saturated because of backend (LLVM) parallelism or by Cargo compiling multiple crates in parallel. So the final performance effect will vary heavily based on the workload that you are running, and on the number of cores that you have available.

We also benchmarked cargo check end-to-end (checking the whole crate graph) on the cargo crate itself on a machine with 8 CPU cores. With 8 threads, it resulted in a ~15% end-to-end improvement:

As can be seen from the results above, when the CPU cores are already saturated with parallel crate compilation and LLVM, the positive effect of the parallel frontend is reduced.

At the start, the nightly toolchain will default to the parallel frontend using only 2 threads. This is a conservative choice that should still allow us to find potential issues while not increasing memory usage a lot at the same time.

If you want to test out the performance with different thread counts, you can override the number of threads used for the frontend using the --jobs-frontend compiler flag. It can be specified either in the RUSTFLAGS environment variable, or you can put it into a .cargo/config.toml file:

Currently, the performance of the parallel frontend will likely not scale very well above ~8 threads, but you can try it on your workload to test what happens. Note that using higher thread counts will likely lead to higher memory usage of the compiler, and in extreme cases it might cause you to run out of memory.

Due to the used parallelism, the produced order of diagnostics might not be deterministic when using the parallel frontend.

In some situations, the generated binary might also not be reproducible, though we currently consider these cases bugs, and we would like to identify them and fix them.

There are currently some known issues related to the reproducibility of the Rust compiler when using the parallel frontend, which are being worked on.

To reiterate: this is only being enabled on nightly for now. If you are using the stable toolchain, you will still be using the sequential frontend by default.

If you want to disable the parallel frontend on the nightly channel, pass -Zunstable-options --jobs-frontend=1 to rustc, either via the RUSTFLAGS environment variable, or with the .cargo/config.toml configuration file:

If you have to do this for some reason, please do tell us why on GitHub or on Zulip. We would especially like to know about any compiler crashes that you encounter, or the produced binaries not being reproducible when the parallel frontend is enabled.

Over the next few months, we will be monitoring GitHub and Zulip for any reported issues about the parallel frontend. Once we have enough confidence that it is working well, and there are no major issues, we would like to move forward and finally stabilize it.

We would also like to improve its performance, and make more things parallel. So far, a lot of the work on the parallel frontend has been focused on making it work correctly, rather than tuning its performance down to the last percent. We thus expect that we might still be able to make further performance improvements to it.

We would also like to make more parts of the frontend actually parallel, as some parts are currently still sequential even if parallelism is enabled. There is some ongoing work on this. Last year, we had a Google Summer of Code project focused on enabling parallel macro expansion and name resolution, and there is also an open pull request for parallelizing the lowering of the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) to the High-Level Intermediate Representation (HIR). More work remains to be done on this front.
