InfoQ Homepage Podcasts Getting CRA Compliant Hardens the Code and Gets Your Company Closer to Digital Sovereignty

In this episode, Christopher "CRob" Robinson, CTO of OpenSSF, Akrites and Chief Security Architect of the Linux Foundation, explores the state of software supply chain security amid multiple security incidents and explains how tools like Scorecard, the Security Baseline framework, and SLSA help harden software.

The conversation also delves into the impact of global cybersecurity regulations like the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), digital sovereignty, and the role of AI in software engineering. Chris shares insights on OpenSSF's Cyber Reasoning System, practical guardrails for AI-assisted development, and how open-source projects are adapting AI contribution policies.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Olimpiu Pop: Hello, everybody. I'm Olimpiu Pop, an InfoQ editor, and I have with me Christopher Robinson, who goes by CRob these days. I'll let him introduce himself and share a bit more background.

Christopher Robinson: Hello, everybody. Thank you for having me today. My name is Chris Robinson, also known as CRob. I am the CTO and Chief Security Architect for a couple of Linux Foundation projects. First, the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF), which focuses on application security, supply chain security, and AI security—predominantly helping support upstream maintainers. My other role is leading a new project called Akrites, which is an upstream open-source coordinated incident response team.

Olimpiu Pop: That sounds like a lot! You wear multiple hats, as people often see in your presentations.

Olimpiu Pop: OpenSSF is definitely a stronghold for security. Before the recent surge in AI, there was a strong push to move security to the left—getting tools and practices closer to development teams. Historically, security was often left for the end alongside documentation and other crucial tasks.

In my experience, whenever something bad happened, the security architect had to scramble down, fix it, and then try to convince developers to adopt the fix. As we record this in early November, we've seen widespread scrambling over PyPI incidents and others, as security incidents continue to rise. We saw an example with PHP where maintainers noted they never expected all four conditions to occur simultaneously—yet they did, with AI contributing to that complexity.

Olimpiu Pop: Exactly. When and who should turn to OpenSSF? Who is your target audience?

Christopher Robinson: We focus on two primary personas. First is the upstream open-source developer and maintainer. We provide comprehensive guidance, best practices, tooling, and training to teach software engineers the expected security controls and practices needed to harden their projects and infrastructure. That is our primary audience.

Secondarily, we care deeply about everyone consuming those projects. Sometimes that is another open-source maintainer integrating a project as a dependency, but predominantly it includes downstream manufacturers and enterprises—such as banks, hospitals, and retailers—running their core operations. We offer tools and guidance to help these consumers evaluate and understand the security posture of projects they plan to integrate, such as Scorecard, which we discussed earlier.

Scorecard serves a dual purpose. It helps upstream maintainers choose the right dependencies, and for maintainers looking to demonstrate their security rigor, it acts as a strong public signal showing adherence to security best practices. Consumers can then look for these signals to inform their decisions.

When evaluating two packages for integration into a solution, consumers can select the option with the stronger security posture.

Olimpiu Pop: That aligns with what we discussed regarding Scorecard examining more than just technical aspects. Many recent issues stems from social engineering or oversight—such as typosquatting or version manipulation in the Python ecosystem, where picking the highest available version bypassed protections.

This focus is especially critical now. While recent incidents draw attention, this shift has been building since the pandemic. During that period, many developers focused heavily on building projects, but subsequent industry reports highlight a different trend.

For instance, Sonatype reports showed a decline in open-source project maintenance, opening doors for attack vectors. Aside from Scorecard, what other tool would you highlight? OpenSSF excels at making best practices actionable. Knowing what is good is one thing; operationalizing it is the real challenge. What other tool would you single out?

Christopher Robinson: I'm going to cheat and I'm going to say two.

Christopher Robinson: First, I would highlight our Security Baseline, which represents the next evolution of Scorecard. The Baseline includes 41 recommended security controls and practices. We analyzed global regulations like the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) and frameworks like the NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) to curate a practical list of actions for project maintainers and consumers.

It combines technical configurations—such as enabling branch protection settings on source code repositories—with organizational controls, like publishing a clear security policy or documenting contributor onboarding and maintainer progression paths.

The Security Baseline is structured across three maturity levels. Level 1 is the most straightforward, roughly equivalent to a mid-range Scorecard score, and takes an experienced developer about two hours to implement. It focuses heavily on documentation. While non-profit open-source maintainers are generally not legally bound by cybersecurity regulations like the EU CRA, downstream manufacturers and governments care immensely about compliance.

The EU CRA explicitly exempts open-source maintainers who do not profit from their work. However, commercial consumers must comply. The Security Baseline translates complex regulatory requirements—from the EU CRA, US Executive Orders, and Japanese legislation—into accessible, practical steps for maintainers without requiring them to digest raw legal texts.

By offering a tiered implementation aligned with modern security practices, the Security Baseline makes projects more attractive to downstream consumers. This increased visibility helps attract more contributors, users, feature requests, and code reviews to strengthen the project.

The second framework I recommend is SLSA (Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts), which addresses supply chain provenance, pedigree, and integrity. While Scorecard and Security Baseline focus on code and process quality, SLSA secures the underlying infrastructure—including IDEs, developer workstations, source repositories, CI/CD pipelines, and distribution systems.

SLSA defines progressive levels of maturity to harden development infrastructure. By pairing process-oriented frameworks like Scorecard or Security Baseline with SLSA, organizations can verify how software moves securely through the supply chain and assess infrastructure resilience.

Olimpiu Pop: You mentioned OpenSSF's work around AI. Previously, we expected software development to rely on human engineering skills built over decades. Now, there is a shift toward AI prompting and engineering assistance. How difficult is it to integrate these security frameworks into AI development harnesses?

How is it is to include all this tooling into harnesses because now all our experience transformed itself into harnesses.

Christopher Robinson: It is a fascinating space. LLMs and AI agents have invited a vast group of new stakeholders into software development. Someone with minimal formal software engineering background can now generate code using straightforward prompts. The key is ensuring these workflows incorporate proper security guardrails and harnesses.

While experienced engineers can leverage trained harnesses and best practices, the challenge lies in the influx of new non-developer contributors across accounting, marketing, and operational roles writing code. With frontier LLMs, there is immense excitement to adopt these powerful tools immediately.

In the rush to adopt AI capabilities, teams risk overlooking 50 years of established software engineering discipline and security practices. AI makes it easy to bypass those foundational controls if guardrails are not explicitly built in.

That has been OpenSSF's main focus this year. We brought in a dedicated AI Security Architect to lead the deployment of the Open Source Software Cyber Reasoning System. This framework acts as a modular harness where developers can plug in AI models, fine-tune their operation, and apply specific security skills and domain context.

Looking ahead, our goal is to build modular skills that integrate directly into these AI harnesses. Next year, we plan to release dedicated skills for Scorecard, SLSA, and Security Insights. These tools will enable automated agents to enforce proven security practices during code generation, ensuring more secure software outputs.

Olimpiu Pop: That is great to hear. Recently, when setting up a repository, I had to manually break down Scorecard recommendations and configure them step by step. With my engineering background, I knew how to implement them, but non-technical users focusing purely on product vision need automated triggers to enforce those standards seamlessly.

And those people don't know what's to be expected. And then it's easier for them if something just triggers that point.

Christopher Robinson: In the hands of an experienced senior engineer, LLMs can be transformative—boosting productivity and reinforcing guardrails. However, developers must actively configure and enable those security skills. I am cautiously optimistic, though real challenges remain.

Olimpiu Pop: I see strong enthusiasm at both ends of the spectrum. Senior engineers can move faster without being blocked, while non-engineering teams can build tools independently without navigating traditional engineering bottlenecks.

You also brought up a major regulatory acronym in Europe: the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA).

Olimpiu Pop: There is a common saying that Europe excels at regulation—as seen with GDPR, the AI Act, and now the CRA. At a recent panel you participated in, speakers discussed digital sovereignty alongside ecosystem fragmentation. In open source, we think globally, but regulations like the US Executive Orders and memory-safe language mandates introduced regional variations. What is your global outlook on cybersecurity regulation right now?

And in the open source ecosystem, we are talking about the global world, a global village. If we take a step upwards, because you're obviously looking at the whole global ecosystem, CRA is getting into force slowly, starting from this autumn. It has multiple stages. Then the US used to have at some point some executive order that started everything in terms of hardening software. And then from that point on, we discussed about memory save programming languages.

I know that Australia invests a lot of money. As you mentioned, you have an agenda for this year and for next year. Maybe you can give us a summary, where is the world from the perspective of the cybersecurity?

Christopher Robinson: Having spent decades as a practitioner starting in the heavily regulated banking sector, I appreciate the value of clear compliance frameworks. That perspective made me eager to see the EU CRA take shape.

While regulation brings implementation challenges, the CRA focuses on necessary, long-overdue principles. Like GDPR's emphasis on citizen data protection, the CRA prioritizes consumer protection against software vulnerabilities and unsafe products, which is a commendable objective.

Global jurisdictions are watching the EU CRA closely ahead of its full enforcement date on December 11, 2027. Countries including the UK, India, Japan, and Australia are observing the rollout as they draft their own cybersecurity approaches.

I anticipate other regions introducing CRA-aligned legislation in the coming years. As a practitioner who prefers efficiency over rework, my hope is that international bodies harmonize their standards rather than creating fragmented, conflicting regulatory requirements.

Fragmented rules would create significant friction. For instance, if Europe adopts established standards for Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) while another region mandates a proprietary 86-point criteria list, manufacturers and developers will face conflicting compliance burdens that hinder efficient delivery.

My goal is to see global regulatory efforts align with the core principles of the CRA—whether through formal legislation or executive frameworks—to maintain consistent expectations for developers worldwide.

Olimpiu Pop: That is a crucial point. A key strength of the CRA was the collaboration between regulators and industry leaders to reach consensus. The remaining question centers on implementation and ensuring fair execution across organizations of all sizes.

Recent high-profile security incidents have increased public and corporate awareness of cybersecurity risks. Beyond standard threats, the global context involves active cyber warfare, making robust software defense essential. Hopefully, regulatory and industry efforts continue moving in the right direction.

Christopher Robinson: To tie this back to digital sovereignty: open-source software provides the most reliable foundation for organizations to maintain autonomy and avoid vendor lock-in. Open source allows teams to inspect, fork, modify, and contribute code back to the community, rather than depending on a single commercial vendor.

This flexibility allows organizations to combine best-of-breed tools—such as pairing an open-weight LLM with European cloud hosting, US-developed web servers, or global components—while retaining full transparency and control over their technology stack.

Olimpiu Pop: This aligns with the local-first software movement. Just as European regulation emphasizes user rights, local-first architecture prioritizes data ownership—ensuring users retain control over their data locally rather than relying entirely on centralized cloud providers.

Olimpiu Pop: Regardless of preference, AI tools are now a permanent part of the software landscape.

Christopher Robinson: They are certainly here to stay.

Olimpiu Pop: Some express concern that automated tools will diminish the human role in software creation. Where do you stand on this spectrum—are you optimistic, pessimistic, or somewhere in between?

Christopher Robinson: I consider myself an AI realist and use these tools daily in my work. AI acts as a helpful assistant that accelerates workflows, rather than a replacement for human engineering judgment. Like a fuzzer or a multimeter in electronics, AI is a tool, and the outcomes depend on how effectively it is applied.

It is important to understand what LLMs actually do: they perform statistical predictions based on context rather than reasoning magic, and they can produce incorrect outputs. Their primary strength lies in identifying patterns across vast datasets—a task where human processing is slower.

When applied thoughtfully, AI provides substantial benefits. However, using these tools without understanding underlying security principles risks exposing sensitive personal or corporate data to external models.

As an AI realist, my goal is to help developers maximize the advantages of AI while remaining aware of potential security risks.

Olimpiu Pop: Given the central role of AI in open source, communities are actively debating AI contribution policies. Some projects require strict human authorship, while leaders like Linus Torvalds view AI as another tool to be used with proper oversight. How do you view recommended AI contribution policies for open-source projects?

Use it cautiously, but you have to understand what's there. And so on, so forth. What's your perspective? How do you see the AI policy of ... I don't know, recommend it maybe?

Christopher Robinson: Policies cross open source remain varied. Maintainers face influxes of automated vulnerability reports and AI-generated contributions, leading to different approaches. While projects like the Linux kernel permit AI-assisted code contributions under developer review, smaller projects with fewer review resources may take a more restrictive stance.

AI usage in software development will continue to grow. The priority for open-source projects is to establish clear, explicit contribution guidelines defining their stance on AI tools. Transparent policies allow contributors to choose projects that align with their preferred workflows.

Olimpiu Pop: Thank you for sharing your insights today, Chris. It was a pleasure speaking with you.

Christopher Robinson: Thank you very much for having me. It was great talking with you.

#9799. AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

Researchers unpacked, mapped, and recreated complex software and the Turla malware, raising opportunities and concerns for organizations and cybersecurity analysts.

Mainstream software and malware can be reverse-engineered more easily than ever, thanks to artificial intelligence (AI) tools — something that security researchers are warning has implications for cyber defense, intellectual property (IP) theft, and beyond.

Household applications typically run on hundreds of thousands, if not millions of lines of code. They incorporate hundreds of third-party libraries, gobs of files, and complex webs of interconnected components. Unpacking and mapping it all is exactly the kind of task that was so difficult before AI, but is now totally in range for even small teams and individuals.

Cybersecurity researchers from Intezer recently tested out how easy it is to reverse-engineer software with AI by picking on some high-profile candidates: Slack, Apple's Finder app, and, importantly for security researchers, the Turla malware. Ironically, the malware proved the most difficult to wrangle. They found it only moderately challenging to meaningfully recreate Apple's and Salesforce's proprietary apps from the ground up.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

"It lowers the bar," Intezer senior security researcher and malware analyst Nicole Fishbein says of AI. "In the past, to reverse-engineer a software, you needed experience. You needed to understand Assembly, and it took a lot of time. Now, I don't want to say anyone [can do it], but it is much easier."

As one would when applying AI to any other major task in cybersecurity, to properly reverse engineer a large program, one needs a "harness." A harness is a little mech suit that focuses a model or models on a specific task, provides it whatever tools it needs to perform its task, and defines its various permissions and restrictions.

No matter her target, Fishbein recalls, "Every case required us to build a different harness, just because the [programs] are so different. For example, if in one case you can just ask Claude to reconstruct the source code, in another case Claude will refuse. Or with malware, when I wanted to be very safe and not execute anything, we had a more complex harness with an extra model."

The malware reconstruction harness ended up consisting of a deterministic Python control plane wrapped around a compiler, with a virtual machine, various static analysis tools, and multiple large language models (LLMs). "We have an Orchestrator agent that controls this whole thing and sends tasks to different sub-agents. It takes the whole binary and breaks it into smaller functions, based on what tools like Binary Ninja provide. From there it goes through a process of reconstruction that is done by one agent, and another agent will test the results," she explains.

Related:Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

By the end, Fishbein and her colleague built a Turla replicant featuring its full working pipeline: how it receives and executes commands, its file transfer mechanisms, more or less everything. For malware researchers without overly tight deadlines, she says, "If you can recreate the full picture and not miss any key components, that gives you a lot of information."

Fishbein notes, "When we started this research, something that I had in the back of my mind was people that vibe code apps that mimic other very common apps. I was just curious to see how possible it is" to mimic the source material nearly exactly. It didn't turn out to be exceptionally difficult, though results did vary.

The researchers' Finder simulacrum could support plenty of everyday uses as the real app — various file actions, local search, etc. — but the original didn't reveal enough to allow them to mimic its internal structure precisely.

Slack went over more easily. Whereas Finder relied on files managed by cloud services, and actions whose results depended on other macOS services, Slack offered little that the researchers couldn't easily unpack by reverse-engineering its Javascript source code. They reproduced the full client "very simply," they wrote, though they had trouble precisely reconstructing its server, information about which wasn't so readily obtained. It's possible, too, that a real-life attacker interested in stealing Salesforce's proprietary code, or picking it apart for vulnerabilities, might not put too much stock in the infrastructure side of things anyway.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

On Sept. 10, Anthropic released a report describing how threat actors have been abusing its models. Among other cases, it described significant activity from the Russian threat actor Midnight Blizzard, primarily targeting Ukraine's government, military, and diplomatic staff. As part of its campaign in Ukraine, Midnight Blizzard had stolen a complete, proprietary software development kit (SDK) for a drone vision system. Over a period of "several days," with help from Claude, the advanced persistent threat (APT) reverse engineered it. The target was of course unsurprising, given that drones have contributed massively to the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Elsewhere in the same report, Anthropic described a Chinese campaign whose goals included malware development, reconnaissance against foreign governments' networks, vulnerability discovery in major endpoint security products, and more. To manage so many workflows at once, the actors ran Claude in different workstreams, one of which involved reverse-engineering security products in search of bugs.

In addition to nation-states, Fishbein points to evidence of reverse-engineering lower down on the threat actor totem pole. "We see a lot of malware that all of a sudden will become open source. There is a tendency of taking malware that threat actors see works well, and then either leaking the source code, or just recreating it and making it open source to anyone," she says.

And, of course, AI is helping reverse engineering reach the upstanding masses. Last month, an open source (OSS) tool and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server called "REA" — short for "Reverse Engineer Anything" — became the single most popular program listed on GitHub.

Now that reverse-engineering is so much faster and more attainable for more people than ever, vendors may need to take more caution with their IP. Their first step might be to define what outcomes they wish to prevent, before deciding on defensive measures. For instance, reverse engineers can straightforwardly reproduce the Slack client, but even in that case they'll not be able to recreate its entire implementation. "Right now, what the research shows is that as long as you haven't [exposed] your server-side infrastructure to the customer, you're protected," Fishbein notes.

To protect their source code, ironically, developers might take some pages out of hackers' playbooks. Malware developers (and cautious corporations, historically) have long proven the efficacy of effective encryption, obfuscation — perhaps, even, with help from AI — and other anti-analysis measures in frustrating the cybersecurity defenders interested in reverse-engineering their creations.

"Encryptors or different anti-cheating mechanisms that have been around for a while would also help," Fishbein says, "but it is hard to tell how long they will hold, with every new model [getting better] every month."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9798. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

#9797. A datetime library for Rust

Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success. Jiff automatically handles many common problems related to daylight saving time by putting time zone handling front and center into the API. Jiff has already seen widespread adoption in the Rust ecosystem.

Jiff is pronounced like “gif” with a soft “g,” as in “gem.”

This blog announces the Jiff 1.0 release by giving a tour of its API.

Target audience: Rust programmers who need convenient datetime handling.

Jiff is already used in production in many projects: uv, Cargo, Starship, fd, Nushell, mise, Jujutsu, uutils/coreutils and even as the basis for a Temporal implementation in AWS LLRT. It is time to call it 1.0.

Unless some significant defect is found in Jiff’s API, my plan is to commit to Jiff 1.0 indefinitely. This is important because the intent is for Jiff to be an ecosystem building block that appears in the public API of other libraries. This makes Jiff an attractive public dependency, which means semver incompatible releases are likely to cause significant pain in the ecosystem. They will not be made lightly.

To see a list of breaking changes between Jiff 0.2 and Jiff 1.0, please consult the CHANGELOG.

In programming, a datetime library’s core functionality rests at the intersection of a computer system’s concept of time and a human’s concept of time. The prevailing notion of system time is Unix time. A human’s concept of time is far more complex, but the most popular such model is the Gregorian calendar coupled with either a 12-hour or 24-hour clock. At the core of every datetime library rests some routine for converting between these concepts.

A datetime library typically provides much more than this. Indeed, datetime handling has historically been very difficult. My own belief is that the difficulty comes from poor modeling of the domain. Instead of encapsulating the complexity inside a reusable bundle of code, many datetime libraries pass some or all of the complexity on to its users. Jiff instead tries hard to encapsulate the complexity and make it difficult for users to do something wrong. (Jiff is not the first to do this!)

In this section of the blog, we’ll do some very basic introductions.

To follow along with the examples in this blog, create a new Cargo project with dependencies on jiff and anyhow:

Most examples are a complete self-contained Rust program. Just copy the code and replace whatever is in src/main.rs. Then run the program:

I am loath to present a dictionary. However, the datetime domain is littered with confusable terms, so I think it’s important to orient ourselves on a shared vocabulary. I’ve kept this section as small as possible. (Some terms, like “time zone,” are omitted here because they are best defined through exploration in the sections that follow.)

TAI and leap seconds won’t be a feature of this blog, but they are listed here in order to convey the difference between Unix time and UTC.

As a way to transition into some of the core types of Jiff, I’ve come to think of its datetime types like an onion. In reverse order, we can build up its layers all the way to a ZonedDateTime. So let’s start with more terms, but this time, they are also types in Jiff:

To make this a bit more concrete, we can see what this looks like in code. Since a time zone can map from a civil datetime to an instant in time, one way to create a zoned datetime requires only a civil datetime and a time zone:

Another way to create a zoned datetime requires only a timestamp and a time zone. This is because time zones can also map a timestamp to a particular civil datetime:

Notice how we get the equivalent zoned datetime in both cases, but we come at it from different directions. In the first case, we start with a time that we might see on our clocks and calendars. In the second case, we start with a particular instant in time that we might get from a database or file system or some other system call.

There is one piece missing from the zoned datetime onion examples: the time zone offset. An offset represents the amount of time one must adjust UTC time in order to get civil time. For example, consider the time 2026-11-01T22:30:00 in UTC. In order to get the civil datetime for someone living in New York, one would subtract 5 hours:

Indeed, every zoned datetime has an offset associated with it:

NOTE: The America/New_York string you see in the above example is an IANA Time Zone Database Identifier. The IANA Time Zone Database is a collection of time zone definitions that can be referenced by a short identifier string. Examples: Australia/Sydney, Asia/Tokyo, Europe/Berlin.

When a civil datetime is combined with an offset, then what you get is always an instant in time.

With the concept of an offset introduced, we can now give a more precise definition of a time zone. A time zone is a geographic region in which civil clocks agree and which provides the following:

Both mappings have been demonstrated in prior examples, but the mapping from civil datetime to an offset seems to be rather complicated due to some potential ambiguity. When does that ambiguity arise? An ambiguous offset occurs when the civil datetime either doesn’t correspond to a valid clock time in this time zone (e.g., when clocks are moved ahead for daylight saving time) or where there could be multiple valid clock times (e.g., when clocks are moved backward for daylight saving time).

Let’s look at some examples. In this first example, we’ll take a look at times around the daylight saving time transition from summer time to standard time in New York. In New York, the clocks were “set back” by an hour at exactly 2AM. This caused the 1AM hour to repeat itself.

The above example shows how Jiff resolves the ambiguity when a “fold” occurs, or when there is a time zone transition that moves the civil time backwards. But we can actually dig down into lower level APIs to change how that ambiguity is resolved. By default, Jiff uses a “compatible” strategy that always selects the first repetition of a time in a fold. But other strategies can be selected by using APIs on a TimeZone directly:

The same idea applies to gaps, or time zone transitions where there’s some civil time that gets skipped on civil clocks. For example, on March 8, 2026 at 2AM, civil time skipped ahead to 3AM:

There are two remaining core types, both representing some notion of a duration:

A Span is the preferred duration type to use whenever possible. Here’s a simple example that shows how to get the number of days between two civil dates:

Generally speaking, whenever there is an operation involving a Span, there is an equivalent operation available with SignedDuration:

Notice that in the above example, we actually switched from using a civil::Date to a civil::DateTime. This was done to show how physical time units can be added. But note that the same can be accomplished with a Span, because it combines all units:

In brief, use a Span when you can. But when it’s too bulky or too slow, use a SignedDuration. One of the key benefits of a Span is that since it represents each unit value distinctly, one can preserve the original meaning of a duration. For example, it’s common to represent the runtime of films in minutes, even when the duration exceeds one hour. Indeed, a span of 2 hours is a distinct span from a span of 120 minutes:

The Span::fieldwise routine converts a Span into a value whose units can be compared in a field-by-field fashion. To compare spans based on the actual physical duration they represent, use Span::compare:

This was a very brief introduction to durations in Jiff. They are a lot more powerful than what is shown here. You might even try playing with the examples above to explore its nooks and crannies. We’ll cover their API in more detail in a later section.

Jiff isn’t always the right thing to use. Sometimes you can get by with something simpler.

First and foremost, if you’re measuring the time something takes in a program, you should almost certainly be using monotonic time. This is available via std::time::Instant:

If you do need to compute elapsed time using your system clock, then Jiff is very convenient for that:

But you don’t actually need Jiff for this. A std::time::SystemTime will work perfectly fine:

Where Jiff starts to become useful is when you need something beyond just an integer number of seconds since the Unix epoch. For example, some very hairy math is required in order to convert a SystemTime into an RFC 3339 timestamp like 2026-11-14T21:34:00Z.

As long as you can live in UTC completely, don’t care about local time and can work with Unix timestamps only, then the Rust standard library won’t steer you wrong.

Conversion to and from strings is a major part of Jiff. Jiff’s focus is primarily on interoperability via the following:

What Jiff actually implements is the Temporal RFC 9557 / ISO 8601 grammar for flexible parsing of datetimes from strings. For most use cases, it suffices to think in terms of RFC 3339, RFC 9557 or ISO 8601. But Jiff does support parsing strings that aren’t valid in any of those three specifications. For example, 2026-11-12[America/New_York] parses as if it was 2026-11-12T00:00:00[America/New_York].

In this section, we’ll take a tour of how Jiff does datetime formatting and printing.

Every datetime and duration type in Jiff implements the standard library FromStr and Display traits. This means that it’s natural to parse datetimes:

Parsing is flexible, so even if there are components missing, parsing still succeeds. For example, without minutes or seconds, those components default to zero:

Another example of flexible parsing is that if a string contains another date type, then one can parse that. For example, one can parse a date out of an ISO 8601 datetime:

A ZonedDateTime always uses RFC 9557 syntax, which includes the IANA time zone identifier:

If you want to print a zoned datetime using only RFC 3339 syntax, then you can do so by formatting the timestamp directly with the zoned datetime’s offset:

The Span and SignedDuration types also support the FromStr and Display traits via the ISO 8601 duration format. For example:

Since a Span is a hybrid duration that also supports calendar units, it can parse durations with calendar units and physical time units. A SignedDuration can only parse durations with physical time units:

The ISO 8601 duration format does, however, have some shortcomings that we’ll discuss in the next section.

Because ISO 8601 duration strings enjoy broad support, it is the default in Jiff for both Span and SignedDuration. However, it has two important shortcomings:

The second shortcoming is best seen with an example. Consider a Span that is 2000 milliseconds. If you convert this to an ISO 8601 duration string and then parse it back, you end up with 2 seconds instead:

This might not be desirable for cases where you want a span’s string format to faithfully represent all possible distinct values of a span.

For these two reasons, Jiff comes with its own bespoke “friendly” duration format. The friendly format is non-lossy and is meant to be easier to read for English speakers than the ISO 8601 duration format. Here are some examples that are all valid friendly durations:

Parsing a friendly duration is as easy as parsing an ISO 8601 duration: the FromStr implementations on both Span and SignedDuration support ISO 8601 durations and friendly durations simultaneously:

Printing a friendly duration does require a bit more effort, since it isn’t the default. Instead of Span::to_string(), one can use the “alternative” syntax via Rust’s formatting machinery:

One can also use a lower level friendly printer to customize its output. For example, here’s how to write a span in the friendly format to an existing String using more spacing, longer unit labels and commas separating each unit:

See the jiff::fmt::friendly module for a lot more detail, including a grammar that precisely specifies the format supported.

The POSIX strptime and POSIX strftime routines are far from the ideal way to format and parse datetimes, but they are ubiquitous and most programmers are familiar with them. Because of their ubiquity, and because of the utility of being able to format and parse bespoke datetime formats, Jiff provides implementations of these routines that are mostly POSIX compatible.

Every datetime type in Jiff comes with strptime and strftime routines. For example, to parse a civil date in the US month/day/year format:

Or to format a zoned datetime in a convenient to read representation for English speakers:

Callers can also use lower level APIs from jiff::fmt::strtime to get access to each parsed component individually:

While the above tour should cover most use cases, there are sometimes reasons for exerting more control over parsing or formatting. Or for supporting alternate formats like RFC 2822. The jiff::fmt module is meant to cover these use cases at the cost of more complex APIs. For example, consider parsing an RFC 2822 datetime string from a &[u8] (which lets callers avoid a UTF-8 validation check):

Another example shows how to change the default disambiguation strategy when the provided civil datetime is ambiguous. For example, Sydney, Australia moved the clocks backwards at 2026-04-05T03:00:00 local time. That is, they went from UTC offset +11 to UTC offset +10. So what happens if we try to parse a time on the clock that is repeated as a result?

Here, the first occurrence of 02:30 is selected, just before Sydney leaves daylight saving time. Now, the data itself can actually select the desired offset:

But this happens because there is no ambiguity in the data. Since the offset is supplied, the exact instant in time is known. Going back to 2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney], which is ambiguous because it could refer to two different instants in time, how do we modify the strategy for resolving that ambiguity? We can’t using the standard library FromStr trait, so we instead have to construct our own parser manually, just like we did for RFC 2822 parsing above. This example shows how to do that and all of the different disambiguation options. Remember, UTC offset +11:00 corresponds to the first occurrence of 2026-04-05T02:30 on the clocks of folks in Sydney while UTC offset +10:00 corresponds to the second occurrence.

The jiff::fmt module contains lots of other goodies that we won’t cover here, including, but not limited to:

No section on datetime formatting would be complete without addressing locales. In this context, a locale is a set of user preferences used for formatting datetimes. This is useful when you want to present a datetime to an end user that doesn’t expect standard formats from RFC 3339, RFC 9557 or ISO 8601.

Jiff itself does not provide any facilities for dealing with locales. Instead, users can opt into this support via the ICU4X project. To make conversions between Jiff and ICU4X, the jiff-icu integration crate can be used.

Here’s an example showing how to format a zoned datetime in the fr-LA locale: (You’ll need to run cargo add icu jiff-icu to your project for this to work.)

The ICU4X API has a lot of options for customizing datetime formatting. Exploring it further is outside the scope of this blog.

Jiff provides many methods on its datetime types to make using them as comfortable and error-free as possible.

Every datetime type provides a new constructor that lets callers build it from its constituent parts. In most cases, this constructor is fallible. For example:

Because creating dates is so common, there is a shorthand for doing so when you know the inputs are valid:

That is, civil::date is a const function that will panic if its inputs are invalid. It should only be used with inputs that are known to be valid. It would, for example, be inappropriate to use this with user provided values. Because of the const block above, if you try to provide invalid values, you’ll get a compiler error.

For datetime types that represent an instant in time (i.e., ZonedDateTime and Timestamp), there is also a now() constructor for getting the current time:

In addition to constructors, new date values can be constructed from old date values using the Date::with API:

Once you have a date, there are oodles of APIs available:

Moreover, because of the datetime onion, all of these APIs are also available on civil::DateTime and ZonedDateTime:

These routines on ZonedDateTime also take time zone transitions into account. For example, ZonedDateTime knows that tomorrow() doesn’t always add 24 hours:

NOTE: We’ll talk about date arithmetic in the next section.

When ZonedDateTime::tomorrow() (among other APIs that produce a ZonedDateTime) would land in a gap or a fold, the “compatible” disambiguation strategy is chosen automatically:

To override this behavior, you can drop down to civil datetimes, perform the operation, and then use TimeZone::to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime to control the exact disambiguation strategy:

There are a few other methods of note on date types that are worth mentioning. First is the ability to query for things like, “The Thursday after next” or “The last Sunday of the month.” The former can be answered by the nth_weekday API:

While the latter can be answered by the nth_weekday_of_month API:

Finally, users can access a convenient time series iterator via series:

All of these methods are also available on civil::Date and civil::DateTime, which should make it very natural to move between them.

All datetime types in Jiff support adding and subtracting durations, and finding the span of time between two datetime values. Let’s start with a civil::Date:

Here we make use of the std::ops::Add trait implementation for civil::Date. The downside of using this, though, is that if the date value goes out of range, then it panics. That may or may not be acceptable. But if you’re dealing with user inputs, then you should use Date::checked_add instead:

Let’s take a look at a few other examples involving months and years:

As with other methods on Date, they are also available on ZonedDateTime:

If we take a look at the type signature for ZonedDateTime::checked_add, we can see that it’s actually polymorphic:

Specifically, it accepts anything that can be converted into a ZonedDateTimeArithmetic. In this case, there are From trait implementations for the following types:

This means that ZonedDateTime::checked_add can accept any one of these duration values:

This type of polymorphism is common in Jiff. Here, it is merely used to provide a convenient way to use multiple duration types. But as we’ll see, it’s also used to provide an extension point for configuration options that control how the operation works.

In addition to adding or subtracting durations from datetime values, one can also compute the duration between two datetime values. For example, to get the number of days between two dates:

Similarly, we can use Date::until to compute the span between dates:

Like with Date::checked_add, this routine is also available at ZonedDateTime::until:

Notice though that hours, instead of days, are returned. This is because two ZonedDateTime values might be in different time zones. Since a ZonedDateTime is fundamentally an instant in time, and because days might be of varying length depending on the time zone, defaulting to hours as the largest possible unit means subtracting two zoned datetimes will always succeed. However, we can request larger units in the duration returned by passing additional options. Notably, ZonedDateTime::until is polymorphic:

That is, callers aren’t just limited to passing a ZonedDateTime here, but anything that can be converted to a ZonedDateTimeDifference. Here is one such example, where we can override the largest units returned in the duration:

A ZonedDateTimeDifference provides much more powerful configuration options for rounding the span returned. Take this example, which produces a span with many unit values:

This might be too much precision to show to an end user. Instead, perhaps we’d like to round the span to the nearest half-hour. We can do this by building a ZonedDateTimeDifference explicitly and configuring its options:

Note also that rounding a span takes time zone transitions like daylight saving time into account. For example, let’s take 2024-11-02 17:30 and 2024-11-03 04:45 in New York. Because New York stopped daylight saving time at 2AM on 2024-11-03, the amount of physical time between them is 12 hours and 15 minutes:

Normally, if we rounded to the nearest day, this would round up to 1 day. But since the midpoint of this particular day is actually 12 hours and 30 minutes, this duration will round down to 0 days when we request it:

Next we’ll continue our discussion of rounding, but when applied to datetimes themselves.

Date rounding in Jiff is limited to units of days or lower. Therefore, it’s only available on ZonedDateTime, Timestamp, civil::DateTime, civil::Time but not civil::Date.

A common example for rounding a datetime is to reduce precision. For example, a system clock might provide nanosecond precision, but maybe we only care about the nearest half-hour:

As with rounding spans, rounding a ZonedDateTime is aware of time zone transitions:

Notice that in the above example, our time of 11:45AM is before noon, yet the result still rounds up to the next day. This is because the midpoint for this day is 11:30AM since, by 11:30AM, 12.5 hours have already elapsed because of the repeated 1AM hour in the move away from daylight saving time in New York.

Jiff itself doesn’t support any calendars other than the proleptic Gregorian calendar. One can instead use the ICU4X crate to work in non-Gregorian calendars, and convert between datetime types using the jiff-icu crate: (Use cargo add icu jiff-icu to make this example work.)

The ICU4X API supports many more calendars.

There are 3 potentially confusable datetime types in Jiff:

When should you use each one versus the other?

To a first approximation, if you can use a ZonedDateTime, then that is probably the type you want to reach for. It represents a specific instant in time in a particular geographic location. That is, it has both a Timestamp and a TimeZone.

If you only ever need to work in UTC or just deal with system time, then a Timestamp is probably the right choice. This is useful for representing a specific instant in time that is not connected to any time zone.

A civil::DateTime is useful in contexts where you don’t care about a specific instant in time and when calcuations should be done independent of time zone. For example, when parsing datetime information from a user interface datetime picker.

Remember that both a civil::DateTime and a Timestamp can be converted to a ZonedDateTime by supplying a time zone.

We’ve already seen how to add spans to datetime values and how to get spans as a difference between datetime values. But we haven’t yet explored the APIs available on a Span itself.

First and foremost, we can build a Span through its constructor, which returns a Span with all of its units set to 0:

A Span is both Copy and immutable. We can create new spans through method chaining:

Or we can use the ToSpan convenience trait, which adds methods on integer types for constructing spans:

Note though that methods like Span::hours and ToSpan::hours will panic when the integer is outside the limits of what Span supports. This is fine when your spans are literals in your program, since a panic would indicate a bug. But if your inputs come from an end user, it’s better to use fallible methods:

Spans preserve each individual unit value. This means that 90 minutes and 1 hour 30 minutes, while they represent the same duration, are actually different values in memory:

This permits callers maximum flexibility when it comes to representing durations. This makes it possible to represent durations in a specific unit even when they add up to larger units. For example, the runtime duration of films is typically conveyed in minutes, even when the runtime exceeds one hour. This can be adjusted programmatically using Span::round:

Neither of these examples do actual rounding, despite the name of the API. Instead, since we’re only setting the largest unit, this API is doing unit balancing. Unit balancing is when all unit values rollover into larger units up until the largest configured unit. This works even for calendar units too, but you need to provide a relative date:

Without a relative date, it’s not possible to know how many hours are in a single month. That is, once calendar units are involved, a span cannot be interpreted as a physical duration of time until some context is applied.

The same even applies to days themselves, since days can sometimes be more or less than 24 hours. Take the above example. What happens if we use a zoned datetime as our relative date instead?

Notice that the duration’s hour component changed from 20 to 21. Why? Because we started with 2756 hour in both cases and because 2020-03-29 in Rome was only 23 hours long (in a move from standard time to daylight saving time). That means that one of those days in 3mo 23d was only 23 hours long. So an extra hour needed to be added to make up for it.

The round API can also do actual rounding:

You can also change its rounding mode from the default (“half-expand”, or like you were taught rounding in school) to truncation (or one of several other modes):

One can also specify a rounding increment to round to the nearest unit value. For example, to the nearest half-hour:

Because a Span value cannot easily be compared correctly based purely on its value in memory, a dedicated comparison Span::compare routine is provided:

Also, one can convert a Span to a floating point value in terms of any unit. For example:

Converting to calendar units requires a relative date for the same reasons discussed above:

So far, we’ve explored a good chunk of Jiff’s API. We didn’t talk about every nook and cranny, but I think we’ve covered the most important pieces.

We’ll wrap up by briefly discussing motivation and inspiration.

Whenever I needed datetime handling in Rust, I always got confused. Should I use chrono or time? How do I get my local time from a timestamp? How do I use my system’s time zone database? How do I do calendar arithmetic?

Before I started working on Jiff, this confusion got annoying enough for me to consider writing my own crate. I felt like the APIs of both chrono and time could be improved upon. I personally found the domain quite interesting and so set out to build something better.

Why not improve on an existing solution, like chrono or time, instead of adding yet another choice into the ecosystem? I do think there are material downsides of having too many choices, but I had concluded that both chrono and time (in 2024) had reached a local maximum. Moreover, in 2024, I was not an expert in datetime handling. It took building a datetime library to become one. So convincing crate maintainers to go in a radically different direction would have been a tall order.

Jiff’s design and comparison documentation contain much more detail regarding the motivation and specific examples between Jiff, chrono and time.

Jiff is heavily inspired by Temporal, which is JavaScript’s standard library solution for date and time management. Jiff inherits API design, functionality and even parsing/formatting of datetime values. Note though that Jiff is not and does not aim to be a 100% compatible implementation of the Temporal specification. Jiff is meant to be a Rust ecosystem library first and foremost.

With that said, if you’re familiar with Temporal and Rust, then it’s likely you’ll find Jiff to be a relatively straightforward translation of Temporal’s API to Rust. This example shows how to use Temporal to round a calendar span to the nearest number of days relative to a date:

And here’s the equivalent operation in Jiff:

The main difference between these examples is that Jiff’s duration type is named Span instead of Duration. This was done to avoid confusion with Rust’s standard library std::time::Duration type.

It’s easy to say that without Temporal, Jiff wouldn’t exist in its current form today.

#9796. Manjaro Project e.V. non-profit organization created

Frank Vandermeiren has announced the creation of the Manjaro Project e.V., a nonprofit organization in Germany that is independent of the Manjaro GmbH & Co KG company. This is following a governance struggle that took place earlier this year between a number of Manjaro Linux contributors and Philip Müller, project lead and CEO of the Manjaro company.

At the moment, we are still working on optimizing the new development infrastructure, which was partly necessitated by the ongoing (A.I.) bot attacks against our old infrastructure.

However, as you may have noticed, the last Testing Updates and Stable Updates were initiated by the Manjaro Team without supervision from Philip Müller — with special thanks to @Yochanan for his hard work!

Dennis ten Hoove has indicated that "a transfer of company assets to the e.V. has not yet taken place", and the group's next step is to ready the nonprofit for the transition and "reach out and engage in dialogue with the company".

#9795. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9794. [$] A new generation of futexes

Futexes are a kernel subsystem that provides support for fast mutexes in user space. While futexes can indeed be fast, they are not fast enough for a number of users. Partly as a result of that, the implementation of futexes has grown in complexity over the years, with two basic variants on offer. The desire for faster futexes remains, though, and that inspires new patches, including this series from Suleiman Souhlal adding a third futex class called "futex PING" for "priority inheritance next generation".

#9793. AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

A command in Claude Code inadvertently saves files with credentials and other sensitive data to public Git repositories, creating security gaps for organizations.

AI coding assistants may inadvertently be leaking thousands of secrets to GitHub public repositories, making what seem like routine interactions between developers and these tools a gaping enterprise security risk.

Research from security firm Apiiro found 2,539 credentials across nearly 2,000 public GitHub repositories, with secrets such as database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens, and SSH root logins among the exposed data, according to a recent report published online. Apiiro tracked some of the leaked data to Claude Code, which was, unbeknownst to users, copying secrets to a hidden file and committing them with the rest of the developer's code.

Among specific secrets leaked were "a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key, a production Azure Postgres password, a Square production token, and the owner password of a medical-records database," Apiiro researchers Shmulik Cohen and Matan Giladi wrote in the post.

Related:AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

Most of the secrets belong to individual developers across 63 organizations, "from student groups to startups, software agencies, and established vendors," they wrote.

The issue stems from how coding assistants — Claude Code, in a specific case that the researchers examined — carry out certain commands. "Ask Claude Code to check a database or call an API, and the command it proposes carries the secret from your config file," the researchers explained.

The tool will ask the user before running the command and, if the choice is "Yes, and don't ask again," then "it saves that exact command, secret included, to .claude/settings.local.json inside the project folder," according to the report.

"Nothing in the repo marks that file as private, so it gets committed with the rest of the code," the researchers explained.

The fact that a routine development task creates a security exposure is dangerous for organizations, especially because these AI coding tools are supposed to be helpful, not harmful, notes Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing for database security firm Liquibase.

“A developer approves a command to save time, the AI agent retains credentials as part of that approval, and those credentials can eventually end up in a public repository," he observes via email. "Nobody intended to expose them, but the workflow made it possible."

In the case of Claude Code, Apiiro examined 104,185 publicly accessible copies of .claude/settings.local.json on GitHub, finding that 1,122 files contained real secrets. The researchers identified 1,379 distinct secrets in those files alone, including 636 provider-specific keys and 743 passwords or tokens associated with public hosts.

Related:People Are Getting Weird About AI

Claude Code is not being overtly careless; it does try to protect files when it creates its .claude/settings.local.json file inside a Git repository, the researchers noted. The tool does this by adding the file to the developer's global Git ignore list, which tells Git to ignore the file on that particular developer's machine. This prevents it from being included in routine commits.

However, the protection is not built into the development project itself, and the "ignore" rule does not travel with the repository when it is cloned onto another machine, the researchers noted. "The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it," they wrote.

Moreover, Claude Code itself was sometimes responsible for committing the exposed files. In 539 of the 1,105 repositories containing real secrets that the researchers investigated, a commit co-authored by Claude Code had modified the affected settings file.

The action that exposes these secrets while using Claude Code appears to be a "dead zone" of sorts for developers using AI coding assistants, so they likely have no idea that they've just exposed a secret, observes Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of AI penetration testing firm BreachLock.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

"A 'don't ask again' prompt is a decision to write a credential into a file, and many developers clicking it likely don't know that file exists," he says. "Once it lands in a repository, it sits in a place many secret scanners were never built to check, which appears to be why some of these leaks slipped through."

Apiiro contacted Anthropic about the issue before publishing the findings. After their publication, Boris Cherny, Anthropic's head of Claude Code, said in public comments that although Claude Code historically has not done secrets scrubbing, the company is looking into what it can do to prevent the secrets exposure described by Apiiro, according to Apiiro's report.

Those approaches may be to make sure auto mode catches the exposure, or to build in basic secrets scanning, among other ideas that Anthropic will prototype "to understand the tradeoffs" before shipping something with its next version of Claude Code, Cherny said.

Indeed, the leakage exposes how Claude Code's protection relies heavily on a developer-specific Git setting rather than a safeguard built into the project or the AI coding tool itself, exposing a gap that can turn an ordinary command approval into a persistent credential leak.

To avoid this, Apiiro recommends that developers rotate every credential a file has ever held, and open all fields and delete every rule containing a secret, even if a file was never committed to a project. Meanwhile, security teams should treat all AI agent folders as secret-bearing on laptops as well as in repos, and add them to pre-commit and secret scanning, including history.

"As AI agents become more involved in software development, organizations need to recognize that source code isn't the only thing they need to secure," McCurdy observes. "Agent configuration files, transcripts, and execution histories can contain sensitive information, and traditional security checks may not catch everything."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.
