#9745. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

#9743. Sola Security Brings Prof. Randall Balestriero on Board to Explore World Models for Cybersecurity

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

The next stage of enterprise cybersecurity may depend on a capability that goes beyond identifying threats: understanding how an organization's technology environment works as a connected system.

A compromised identity, for example, can create risks that extend beyond the account itself. Determining which workloads it can access, how its permissions interact with infrastructure, and what could happen if those permissions are revoked requires an understanding of relationships across an enterprise environment.

Sola Security believes this kind of contextual understanding could shape the next generation of cybersecurity agents. In a press release announcing its latest research appointment, the company said it has brought Prof. Randall Balestriero onto its scientific advisory board to advance that vision.

Balestriero is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Brown University and a visiting researcher at Meta AI Research (FAIR). He has worked alongside renowned AI researcher Yann LeCun and co-authored research with him. His work focuses on self-supervised learning and representation learning, including how AI systems develop structured representations of the world around them.

At Sola, he will advise on research directions that connect these foundational AI concepts with the everyday challenges of enterprise security.

Enterprise security environments contain interconnected identities, permissions, workloads, and infrastructure dependencies. Yet many security questions cannot be answered by examining a single suspicious event or configuration.

Identifying a compromised identity, for instance, does not automatically reveal the full extent of its access. Security teams need to understand which workloads that identity can reach and how its permissions relate to other components.

The response itself can introduce additional operational considerations. Revoking access may affect other systems or workloads, making it important to understand what could break before implementing a change.

This creates a distinction between detecting a security problem and understanding its implications.

Sola's approach centers on the idea that AI agents need a continuously updated representation of the environments they protect. Instead of processing disconnected findings, agents should be able to understand how different components relate and evaluate the potential consequences of proposed actions.

The concept of world models is central to Sola's research direction. The company sees new types of models capable of understanding environments and relationships as a potential foundation for more advanced cybersecurity agents.

Applied to enterprise security, these principles could help AI systems build comprehensive representations of organizational environments. An agent could potentially reason about how identities connect to workloads, what permissions actually enable, and how a security intervention might affect other parts of an organization.

This would change the role of an AI security agent.

Rather than simply responding to an alert, an agent with a deeper understanding of its environment could evaluate different possible actions and consider their downstream effects. The objective is to make decisions with greater awareness of operational context.

For example, an agent identifying a compromised identity would need to do more than flag the account. It would need to understand the identity's potential reach, assess the consequences of removing its access, and determine an appropriate response.

That distinction is important as enterprises increasingly introduce AI agents into security operations, where investigating threats, managing access, and carrying out remediation actions can involve interconnected systems.

Balestriero's appointment brings expertise in representation learning and self-supervised learning into Sola's research efforts.

His work examines how AI systems develop structured representations of the world around them. Sola intends to explore how perspectives from this area of foundational AI research can inform the development of security agents capable of understanding complex enterprise environments.

Guy Flechter, Co-Founder and CEO of Sola Security, believes the industry needs to rethink what it expects from security systems.

"Cybersecurity has spent years building systems that can identify problems, but understanding the environment behind those problems is an entirely different challenge," said Flechter. “We believe the next generation of security agents will need something closer to a world model: an understanding of how systems connect, how changes propagate, and what the consequences of an action will be before it is taken.”

He also emphasized the value of bringing Balestriero's research perspective into the company's work.

"Randall brings a depth of expertise in how AI systems learn representations of the world. Bringing that perspective into cybersecurity is an important step for us. We want to build agents that don't just react to what they observe, but understand the environments they protect and can reason about the impact of their decisions."

The appointment reflects Sola's position as a research-driven cybersecurity lab focused on the intersection of foundational AI research and enterprise security.

Rather than limiting innovation to adapting existing AI models for established security workflows, the company is exploring how advances in AI could enable systems to understand relationships, dependencies, and potential outcomes.

As AI agents take on more responsibilities in enterprise security, this distinction could become increasingly significant. Systems that understand the environments they operate in may be better positioned to assess risks and evaluate the consequences of their actions.

For Sola, bringing Balestriero onto its scientific advisory board is a step toward exploring that possibility.

#9742. Huskeys Taps Former HackerOne CCO Eyal Kaldes to Run Its Customer Organization

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Huskeys has a new executive in charge of making sure its customers succeed.

The Network Edge Security Management (NESM) company announced in a press release that it has hired Eyal Kaldes as Chief Customer Officer, putting him in charge of its customer strategy and the entire post-sale organization. Kaldes arrives with more than 20 years of customer success and post-sales leadership across enterprise security, networking and AI, most recently as Chief Customer Officer at HackerOne.

His brief is simple to state and big in scope: help enterprise customers get measurable value out of the Huskeys platform, from the day they first deploy it to the point where they are running NESM at scale.

At HackerOne, Kaldes ran a post-sale operation with an unusually wide footprint. Customer success, professional services, technical support, triage and vulnerability validation, onboarding and community all sat inside his organization.

That is a serious pedigree. HackerOne is a global cybersecurity leader and a pioneer of crowdsourced security, connecting organizations with ethical hackers through bug bounty programs so they can find vulnerabilities. The company has played a major role in shaping how enterprises approach vulnerability discovery and security testing.

Earlier in his career, Kaldes led client services at PerimeterX and served as GM and Vice President of Client Services at Aerohive Networks, supporting more than 30,000 customers through a global network of more than 500 resellers and distributors and working alongside strategic partners such as Dell.

He also holds a seat on the Customer Success Advisory Board of CloudShare.

At Huskeys, Kaldes becomes the most senior Israeli executive on the team, according to the company. Along with his leadership experience, he brings a strong connection to the Israeli cybersecurity ecosystem.

Itai Gafni, CEO and Co-Founder of Huskeys, tied the hire directly to what the company has learned by working closely with its customers.

"Working side by side with our customers, we saw that the edge had become the most critical and least managed layer of the enterprise, and that organizations need NESM now," Gafni said.

He went on to explain why Kaldes was the pick. "Our job is to make sure every step of our customers' journey delivers real, measurable protection. Eyal has built customer organizations for some of the world's largest enterprises and scaled them through rapid growth. He brings a rare combination of cybersecurity depth, operational leadership and a genuine obsession with customer outcomes, and he is exactly the leader we need to keep every Huskeys customer ahead of what's coming at the edge."

Huskeys is building an NESM platform that helps organizations understand, manage and secure network edge environments, which keep growing more complex in the agentic AI era. The platform does not ask companies to rip out the tools they already rely on. Instead, it connects and orchestrates existing CDNs, WAFs, cloud security and other network edge technologies through a single unified agentic layer.

What customers get is continuous assessment, plus the ability to dynamically adapt policies, reduce exposure and protect business-critical applications at scale.

A platform with that kind of reach puts a premium on the team that helps customers roll it out and grow with it. The appointment reflects Huskeys' focus on building a customer organization that can scale alongside the business and keep pace with evolving market needs.

Kaldes sees a clear shift in who, and what, is driving traffic at the edge.

"AI agents now drive a growing share of edge traffic, and security teams are being asked to protect it faster and with less visibility," he said. "The enterprises I've worked with don't just want a platform. They want a partner who gets them to outcomes quickly. My focus is building a customer organization at Huskeys that delivers that from day one and scales as the company grows."

In practice, his work will center on helping customers reach meaningful outcomes while setting up the processes and relationships that support long-term partnerships. For Kaldes personally, the role is a chance to use his experience across several stages of the customer lifecycle and to help shape what comes next for Huskeys in the world of AI.

The bottom line for Huskeys customers: the person now running their experience has spent more than two decades doing exactly that, at enterprise scale.

#9741. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#9740. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

#9739. Energy-Based Models for Enterprise Decision-Making: Architecture and PyTorch Implementation

Director, Engineering | Driving Innovation from Ideation to Execution | AI, Cloud-Native & IoT | Technology Strategy & Design Thinking

Director, Engineering | Driving Innovation from Ideation to Execution | AI, Cloud-Native & IoT | Technology Strategy & Design Thinking

Director, Engineering | Driving Innovation from Ideation to Execution | AI, Cloud-Native & IoT | Technology Strategy & Design Thinking

Enterprise AI has become quite good at prediction. Given a food-delivery order, a machine-learning model can estimate the delivery time. A retailer can forecast demand for the next week. Large Language Models (LLMs) added another capability. They can understand unstructured information, generate content, summarize documents, interact with users and perform reasoning tasks.

But many enterprise problems do not end with prediction or reasoning. Eventually, the system has to decide:

This is where decision systems become important. Recently, System One models have been proposed for fast, structured decision-making. TypeSafe AI, for example, positions Jev as a System One model that accepts state and typed questions and returns structured probabilistic answers.

Another approach worth examining is the Energy-Based Model (EBM). EBMs are not new. The concept has been studied for several decades. What makes them relevant to enterprise architecture today is their ability to score possible outcomes or actions instead of simply producing one prediction.

This article looks at where Energy-Based Models can fit alongside traditional machine learning, LLMs and emerging System One models.

Consider a simplified DoorDash-like food-delivery system. The platform wants to estimate how long an order will take to reach the customer.

A conventional machine-learning model might use:

A regression model learns f(x)=y, where x represents the current marketplace state and y represents delivery duration.

The model might return f(x)=43.7 minutes that is useful. But it is not necessarily the final business decision. Should the application tell the customer "Your order will arrive in 44 minutes"?. Not necessarily. Being five minutes late may damage the customer experience more than providing a slightly conservative estimate. The platform therefore has to answer a different question:

What delivery time should we promise the customer?

And the real operational problem is even broader. The delivery platform may also need to determine:

These are related questions, but they are not the same as predicting one number.

Which possible state, outcome or action best fits the situation and our objectives?

Consider the following probability distribution of delivery time for one-order (the 60-minute slot covers deliveries of 60 minutes or more):

The most preferred selection is around 45 minutes (higher probability - 27%). But suppose being late is much more damaging to customer experience than giving a conservative estimate. The best customer promise might be 50 minutes (though only 24% likely). The prediction remains 45 minutes. The decision might be 50 minutes. Hence “Models estimate reality. Decision systems choose actions.” Traditional machine learning primarily helps with the first problem. Decision systems must solve the second.

The below scenario illustrates the use of EBM:

An Energy-Based Model learns an energy function:

It is the energy assigned to candidate y given context x. The symbol theta (θ) represents the model parameters such as neural-network weights and biases - the model learned from historical data. Hence, if Energy function returns 0.5, that can be read as:

"Using the parameters learned during training, the model assigns energy 0.5 to the combination of this marketplace state and a 45-minute delivery."

Lower energy indicates that the candidate is more compatible with the current context. Higher energy means it fits poorly. Hence, Inference can therefore be expressed as:

This is different from asking a model to directly predict one value. Instead, we can evaluate several possible values or actions and ask: Which candidate fits this situation best?

Imagine placing a ball on an uneven surface. The ball naturally tends toward a valley.

An EBM creates something conceptually similar: a landscape over possible solutions. The EBM is learning the shape of the solution landscape. Instead of knowing only where the valley bottom is, we also know something about the terrain around it. For the delivery example, the model might assign:

A normal regression model might simply say:

The EBM instead says something closer to:

This is a subtle but important difference. The model is learning the shape of the solution space, not merely returning one scalar value.

For a finite set of candidate delivery durations, we can convert energies into normalized probabilities:

Applying this formula to the eight energies from the previous section gives the distribution below (probabilities rounded to the nearest percent). For example, for 45 minutes: e^(-0.50) = 0.607, the eight terms sum to 2.244, and 0.607 / 2.244 = 27%. This is the same distribution as the opening chart, with its 60-minute slot (9%) split into 60 minutes (7%) and 65 minutes (2%).

From this distribution: Mode=45 minutes; the median (P50) is also 45 minutes because cumulative probability crosses 50% at 45 minutes. Similarly: P90=55 minutes. We now have more information than a single ETA. But there is an important point here.

Traditional machine learning already provides strong techniques for uncertainty estimation. Quantile regression can directly estimate P50, P80 and P90. Probabilistic regression can estimate a complete probability distribution. LightGBM, XGBoost and neural-network-based approaches can all be used for this purpose. Hence, generating a probability distribution around an ETA is not sufficient justification for introducing an EBM.

An EBM becomes more interesting when the candidate being evaluated is richer than a single number. Before getting there, however, let us look at how prediction becomes a decision.

Suppose the business decides that being late is four time more costly than providing a conservative ETA.

Let (a) = actual delivery duration, (p) = promised delivery duration. Define the business cost as:

Now the system should not simply select the most likely ETA. It should choose the promise that minimises expected business cost. In our example:

Evaluating the expected cost of each candidate promise against the distribution above gives E[C(a,50)] = 11.5 for a 50-minute promise and E[C(a,55)] = 10.5 for a 55-minute promise. Every other candidate costs more (45 minutes: 18.5; 60 minutes: 13.25). Among these discrete candidates, the optimal customer promise is therefore 55 minutes. This agrees with the classic critical-ratio result: when being late costs four times as much as being early, the best promise is the 4 / (4 + 1) = 80th percentile, and 55 minutes is the first candidate whose cumulative probability (91%) reaches 80%.

However, quantile regression could also solve this particular problem by directly estimating P80. So we need to go one step further to understand where an EBM can provide a more distinct capability.

Until now, y represented only delivery duration. What happens if y represents an entire operational plan?

The platform may have several possible plans:

The energy function now becomes: E_theta({marketplace state}, {delivery plan}). Conceptually:

This is a stronger EBM use case. The model is no longer estimating uncertainty around one scalar value. It is scoring possible operational states and actions as illustrated below.

Take the three candidate plans from the previous section, now with their estimated route durations:

The EBM's job is to score these actions and identify the one that best fits the current marketplace state.

The context describes the current situation. For example:

The action describes what we could do. For this simplified example, assume that each candidate action has numerical features such as:

A simple PyTorch model can concatenate the context with each candidate action and return one scalar energy per candidate. It scores a whole batch of decisions at once, which is how it is trained and served:

Unlike regression, the energy model does this:

context + candidate duration → Energy Model → energy

Step 3: Generate Feasible Candidate Actions

Assume the operational system generates three feasible plans for one marketplace state. Route and promise minutes are divided by 60 so that every feature sits on a similar 0–1 scale; the same scaling must be applied during training:

Now evaluate each candidate against the same marketplace context. Plans that break a hard constraint are masked out so they can never be selected:

Step 5: Train Good Actions to Have Lower Energy

The model still has to learn what constitutes a good action. Suppose historical data, an operational simulator, or another trusted decision process tells us that Action B produced the best outcome for a particular marketplace state.

We want: E_theta(x,A_B) < E_theta(x,A_A) and E_theta(x,A_B) < E_theta(x,A_C)

One convenient implementation is to treat negative energy as the candidate logit and apply a cross-entropy loss across the candidates of each decision, the same contrastive objective used to train energy-based policies in Implicit Behavioral Cloning. In practice the model learns from many logged decisions, each with its own context, its own set of feasible candidates and the index of the best one:

The training process adjusts (theta) so that preferred actions receive lower energy.

There is an important practical consideration here. The historical action is not automatically the best action. If a historical dispatcher selected Dasher D42, that does not prove D42 was optimal. Training labels should therefore come from a suitable source such as:

Otherwise, the EBM may simply learn to reproduce historical decision-making mistakes.

Step 6: Convert Energy Into Action Probabilities

If we are comparing a finite set of candidate actions, we can convert their energies into probabilities:

Action B receives the highest probability because it has the lowest energy. These are normalized model scores over these three candidates, not necessarily calibrated probabilities of real-world success.

System One Models and Energy-Based Models should not automatically be treated as competing technologies. TypeSafe describes Jev, its first System One Model, as taking state and typed questions and returning typed probabilistic decisions. Unlike an autoregressive LLM, which generates strings token by token, Jev is designed around structured outputs and parallel sampling.

TypeSafe reports approximately 70–500 ms end-to-end response times and 40×–200× speed improvements for comparable System-One-shaped queries in some of its demonstrations. In our delivery example, a System One model might rapidly classify the marketplace state:

This judgment can influence which actions should even be considered. The Energy-Based Model then compares possible responses within that context. This can be interpreted as “System One narrows the interpretation of the world. Energy-based scoring compares possible responses to that world”.

LLMs remain extremely useful because enterprise information is often messy and unstructured. Suppose a restaurant manager writes:

"Heavy rain around the store. Two riders cancelled, kitchen is running about 15 minutes behind and we suddenly have 23 open orders."

An LLM can transform this into structured state:

That state can feed predictive and decision models. The LLM can also explain the final decision:

"The delivery promise was extended because the restaurant is currently delayed, driver availability is low and heavy rain is increasing expected travel time."

This leads to an architecture in which each model does what it is good at.

You can also build an EBM on top of a small LLM such as gemma-3-270m or Qwen3-0.6B. The idea is simple: use the LLM only to read, not to write. Describe the context and one candidate as a short piece of text, pass it through the model, and add a small layer on top (the “energy head”) that turns the model’s internal representation into a single energy score. The model’s text generation ability is not used at all.

This approach is useful when the candidates or the context contain free text: dispatcher notes, restaurant messages, or constraints written in plain language. A small LLM already understands such text, so you do not have to convert it into numeric features by hand. Gemma 3 270M is the lighter and faster option; Qwen3 0.6B is about twice the size and gives somewhat richer representations at a higher cost.

For purely numeric inputs, like the food delivery example in this article, a plain MLP (multilayer perceptron) is the better choice. It is faster and usually more accurate, because LLMs of any family handle numbers poorly when they are written as text. Switching from Gemma to Qwen does not change this.

A practical middle path is a hybrid: let the LLM read only the text part of the context, and feed the numeric features straight into the energy head.

None of these components has to replace all the others. The interesting architecture is often a composition of them.

An EBM can be a small neural network like the PyTorch example above. It does not require GPT, Claude, Llama or another LLM. For a structured enterprise problem such as pricing, scheduling, delivery planning or inventory allocation, I would often prefer a separate, domain-specific energy model. However, energy functions can also be built around large language models (References #7).

Unlike LLMs provided via closed APIs (OpenAI's GPT or Anthropic's Claude), Energy-Based Models are rarely offered as turnkey cloud APIs. This is due to the inherent computational difficulty of inference-time optimization (finding low-energy states typically requires iterative sampling or gradient descent loops at runtime). Instead, they are actively researched, custom-built, and integrated into specialized domain software such as autonomous vehicle trajectory planners, robotics policy optimizers, and advanced self-supervised world model architectures.

#9738. AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

An organization's ability to quickly recover from a business disruption will be a competitive advantage in an era of AI-driven threats and business enablement.

Commvault SHIFT — Nashville, Tenn. — Enterprise data recovery practices must evolve from a last-resort response to a continuous operational discipline focused on minimizing business disruption and containing the blast radius of cyber incidents as quickly as possible.

That was the central message at Commvault's SHIFT 2026 conference this week, where security executives highlighted the growing importance of making operational resilience a business priority as AI-driven threats and increasingly autonomous business processes complicate the task of maintaining continuity.

"AI is changing the durable advantage you have built for your business, your brand, your supply chain, your data," said Sanjay Mirchandani, president and CEO of Commvault, in a keynote address at the event. "In the AI era, resilience will be your new competitive advantage."

Two developments are driving the trend. On the threat side, AI is giving attackers the ability to automate and accelerate reconnaissance, exploit development, social engineering, and lateral movement. The trend has compressed the time organizations have to detect and contain an intrusion, Mirchandani and other executives at the event noted.

Related:AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

At the same time, enterprises are increasingly embedding AI into business processes, workflows and decision-making, creating new dependencies on data, applications and autonomous systems.

The result is a more complex operating environment in which a disruption can have wider and faster consequences, making the ability to contain incidents, preserve trusted operations and recover without derailing business activity more important than ever.

Attackers these days are able to move faster with a level of automation not available before, noted Rajeev Kottomtharayil, chief products officer at Commvault. Increasingly, recovery is becoming not just about speed but bringing back clean data. "If everything is under attack, how do we know what to trust? The real goal is to have a clean, safe space to recover even if everything around you has been compromised," Kottomtharayil said.

Business innovation and enablement are also driving the need for greater operational resilience. Resilient operations give organizations the confidence to experiment with AI and put it to work across the business, while ensuring they can recover quickly when something goes wrong, said Pragnesh Dave, head of generative AI and ML sales at AWS. "AI is collapsing the amount of time it takes to move from an idea to an outcome," he said during a keynote session. As a result, the competitive advantage will come not simply from how quickly organizations can turn intelligence into action, but from how quickly they can do so while managing the risks and consequences when those actions sometimes prove wrong.

Related:People Are Getting Weird About AI

Dave pointed to the operations model at Amazon that emphasizes the notion of the "door swinging both ways" when teams try to innovate. It is an approach that has enabled teams at Amazon to code more than four times faster than before, he said.

"The question for everyone is not if something is going to break," he said. Rather, it is about what the blast radius is and the time it takes from when something breaks to recovering to the prior trusted state. "If something goes wrong, you need to be able to recover quickly. You should be able to walk back a decision. Think of your recovery time as your innovation project."

Continuous detection and continuous recovery are going to become a baseline requirement for organizations, argued Peter Diamandis, futurist, entrepreneur, and founder and chairman of the XPRIZE Foundation. Over the next few years, he foresees all organizations harnessing AI to migrate a significant workload to the "digital edge" with humans providing judgement, taste, and oversight. "AI gives us all access to capabilities that were once scarce." The qualities that matter the most will be the speed at which an organization can innovate and that requires standing up capabilities to recover quickly when failures do occur, he said during a keynote address.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

At the same time, recovery is not becoming a substitute for prevention, says Bill O'Connell, chief security officer at Commvault. Both are equally important. But "building the highest walls and the deepest moat" to keep threats out alone is no longer enough. Organizations have to equally focus on building an ability to recover quickly to a trusted state regardless of the reason for a disruption and to thoroughly test that ability before it becomes necessary.

The key to keep in mind is that while AI has dramatically accelerated the pace of change it hasn’t altered the need for traditional, and long-familiar, IT governance and controls around their assets, identities, access, authentication and authentication, O'Connell says. "The IT maintenance and housekeeping elements still matter." When organizations have supercharged tools which they are not entirely sure how to govern, they need to make sure those fundamentals remain in place.

In enabling better resilience, organizations should also evaluate what impact third parties could have on their ability to quickly restore operations, O'Connell says. For years, organizations have used questionnaires and external vendor risk-scoring services to try and assess third-party risk. In the AI era, security teams need to go a step further with their most critical suppliers, he adds. O'Connell suggested organizations have their technical architects work with their counterparts at third-party suppliers to understand how critical services are actually configured and what would happen if a provider experienced a breach or a disruption.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9737. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9736. Relationships Are Becoming Web3's Most Valuable Infrastructure

Caroline Moellers is the Chief Communication Officer at Seasons ($SEAS). A former film Assistant Director who transitioned to crypto in 2018, she le

Caroline Moellers is the Chief Communication Officer at Seasons ($SEAS). A former film Assistant Director who transitioned to crypto in 2018, she le

Caroline Moellers is the Chief Communication Officer at Seasons ($SEAS). A former film Assistant Director who transitioned to crypto in 2018, she le

The past decade and a half has seen the crypto sector build systems designed to take trust out of the equation entirely, so much so that once two parties agree to a transaction, a smart contract settles the deal, and neither side needs to know, or even like, the other.

However, what none of that code can do is decide who belongs in the deal to begin with, i.e. which founder gets funded, which project gets integrated and which partner gets the first call. All of these decisions are still made by people, and people tend to back those they know or those someone they trust has vouched for.

Ask almost any founder as to how their last round came together, and the answer usually starts with someone who made an introduction, took a call they didn't have to take, or remembered a favor from two cycles ago.

In effect, while the technology was built so strangers could transact without trusting each other, yet the business of building on it still runs on relationships, arguably more now than at any point before.

For a brief moment during the 2021 boom, it looked as though the aforementioned status quo might have changed, given that capital was so plentiful. As a result, a half decent deck and a busy Discord was all that was needed to close a seed round.

Introductions mattered less because hardly anyone was saying no; however, over the last couple of years, that window has firmly shut. Galaxy Research counted only five new crypto venture funds closing in the second quarter of 2026, the fewest since 2019, while roughly 78% of the quarter's capital went to later-stage companies with track records.

Fewer investors are writing checks, and they are writing them to teams they already know or to teams that someone they trust has vouched for. Consequently, the founders who are struggling the most in this market are those who only started networking once they needed something.

The clearest sign that relationships carry real economic value came when someone finally put a price on them. To this point, last October, Coinbase paid roughly $375 million for Echo, the platform Cobie Fish built to let communities invest together in private rounds. By the time of the sale, participating projects had already raised more than $200 million via it (spread across about 300 deals).

From the outside looking in, one can see that by stripping away Echo’s onchain plumbing, its core asset was simply ‘trust.’ People put money into deals because someone they respected was already in them and that is the idea that will likely define the industry’s near to mid term future.

The trouble, as things stand, is that a large part of Web3 still treats relationships as transactions with a handshake attached. Partnerships get announced on X with two logos and a fire emoji, then quietly forgotten within a month.

Anyone who has worked in crypto communications has watched this happen from the inside where the announcement becomes the deliverable, and nobody checks whether the two teams actually spoke again after the press release went out.

But it is worth remembering that memories in this industry are long and the cast of characters in this space is far smaller than it looks from the outside. The same faces turn up at every conference from New York to Dubai to Singapore, and reputations travel faster than any token.

That is what earns relationships the label of infrastructure because the physical ones can take years to build and only get noticed when they fail.

In closing, while the protocols themselves may be trustless, the people building them never will be, and the teams that accept that early will be the ones still standing (and forging long term deals) when the next cycle does eventually come along.

#9735. Attackers Say 'Hello' to a Different Scale of Cloud Attack

Researchers dubbed an attack chain "Greeter" after discovering that attackers deliberately covered their trail by leaving "hello" messages in logs.

What began as an exploratory Shodan search for exposed cloud instances has led to the discovery of a broad-ranging AI infrastructure attack campaign that researchers have christened "Greeter." The campaign, which started life as an organized, multistage, systematic attack across cloud providers, reinforces why defenders need to shift their thinking about cloud security to include a layered model built around network access control, data protection, and identity security.

Era Security researchers kicked off the research when the Shodan search engine revealed open Amazon DynamoDB instances where anyone could download data or delete it entirely. They dug a little deeper and found Flowise, a connected open source GenAI development platform, where users can build AI agents powered by large language models (LLMs).

Roughly 90% of the nearly 3,000 scanned Flowise deployments were running unpatched versions vulnerable to a critical code-injection vulnerability, CVE-2024-58351 — and if the researchers could see it, so could attackers. So, Era Security deployed AI-powered honeypots, mostly on Amazon Web Service (AWS), to catch them in action.

Related:LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

Honeypot technology is "not like it was before," and attackers don't recognize it's a decoy until they're much further into the environment, according to the Era Security research team. In the past, it took three or fourth months to build a realistic honeypot. Today, it's two hours.

"The most important finding wasn't the exploitation technique itself, but it was what happened after," Naor Talmor, chief technology officer (CTO) at Era Security, tells Dark Reading. What ensued was a repeatable, staged methodology where attackers mapped out privileges and the environment, hunted for credentials, exploited cloud metadata services across multiple providers to escalate access, and then locked in persistence, he explains. Attackers also obfuscated their activity by leaving seemingly benign and fleeting "hello" messages in the logs, making detection much more difficult because it requires team to spend time searching for specific indicators of compromise in the logs. Thus, the researchers gave the campaign the "Greeter" moniker.

The sophisticated techniques and persistence show that Greeter isn't an opportunistic smash-and-grab attack, a script kiddie, or someone who had merely stumbled upon the honeypots, the researchers noted. And, the campaign was deployed across several AWS regions at once, which indicates broader scale and intent.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Era Security warns of the potential scale the campaign could reach, confirming 46 real-world victims so far, based on the number of unauthenticated instances that mirrored the honeypot conditions. The team estimates that at least 50% of those remain connected to the Internet and visible, suggesting at least 20 organizations are currently exposed. The sophistication levels of the the threat actors also speaks to how how valuable the cloud and AI attack surface has become, given the effort required to launch Greeter; this wasn't low-hanging fruit.

The Greeter campaign signals a few shifts across the cloud landscape, including how much easier it's gotten for attackers to go unnoticed in workflows. Much of that is due to AI, which threat actors are using to assist in writing code or orchestrating attack steps, according to the Greeter attack logs.

A decade ago, cloud attacks targeted the Docker API. Threat actors then began exploiting workloads, escaping containers to reach the cloud's metadata server underneath, and exploiting service accounts from there, the researchers explain. While attackers are following a similar pattern, they are now using AI infrastructure as the new way to establish persistence.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

Researchers agree that the end goal on each instance was to grab cloud credentials and perform lateral movement within a targeted organization.

Meanwhile, attribution remains quite challenging. When the researchers drilled down to the code and techniques, they started to see Chinese characters, though that could be a false flag. Still, a nation-state culprit would make since, because the notion of seeing an "entire orchestration, not even a big cybercrime group could execute that," according to Era Security.

The current velocity of vulnerability exploitation is nothing like the researchers have seen in the past, which puts immense pressure on organizations' traditional patching cycles. This played out just over the past few weeks alone, as security teams raced to fix PHP2Shell and OpenSSH, searching workloads one by one for flaws. However, the Greeter campaign shows a defense challenge for cloud security that's bigger than fixing any specific vulnerability.

Everyone needs to assume a breach now, warns Talmor, adding how if it's not a vulnerability, it may be leaked credentials or an exposed API. Organizations need to design security programs around the cloud to be ready for all of the above, he advises, adopting defense-in-depth.

"A lot of companies adopt that, but they don't really practice it," he notes.

The researchers say organizations can detect this kind of attack much faster if teams monitor for enumeration activity to close gaps before attackers find them. When applications or chat tools are installed, logging can be activated and streamed to a separate location so that even if attackers do delete a device's local history, the logs remain stored in the cloud.

Researchers also noted that this should be monitored closely in critical environments, especially where crown jewels or critical applications are involved, adding that organizations can have dozens or hundreds of accounts depending on the size.

"To be clear, we aren't saying, 'Stop caring about misconfigurations or stop caring about vulnerabilities," Talmor says, warning that patch management is a game "we are losing" that requires organizations to secure their environment layer by layer.

#9734. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.
