#9710. Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9709. ArcticRAT Cybercrime Gang Profiles Victim Finances With AI

The Android malware has expanded from focusing on cryptocurrency theft to full device control, and the attackers have added advanced analysis of stolen information.

Android cryptocurrency stealer ArcticRAT has evolved into a sophisticated remote access Trojan (RAT) capable of taking control of victim devices, harvesting sensitive information, and using AI to identify valuable financial data.

Researchers at Zimperium who are tracking the malware described it as representing a "dangerous escalation" in the mobile threat landscape. The newer versions, according to the vendor, give attackers the ability to interact with infected devices in real time, rather than relying purely on hardcoded actions.

The malware uses multiple techniques, including a "completely black, un-dismissible" screen overlay to conceal attacker activities from victims. Most significantly, the operators of ArcticRAT are now using large language model (LLM) services to automatically sift through stolen text messages and other data from infected device for financial information worth exploiting.

Related:APT29's Watering Holes Target Thousands of Mobile Users

"ArcticRAT uses AI to read through user information such as SMS messages to filter for financial information that could be used perform fraud," Nico Chiaraviglio, chief scientist at Zimperium, tells Dark Reading. "One particularly challenging technique is hidden remote control combined with a black-screen overlay. Attackers abuse legitimate Android features while making the device appear locked or powered off."

Defending against threats like ArcticRAT requires organizations to deploy AI-powered, on-device threat detection, enforce controls over application installation and permissions, and use runtime application protection to identify suspicious screen-sharing activity and malicious overlays, he adds.

Early versions of ArcticRAT targeted users of 11 specific cryptocurrency applications. Its primary purpose was to harvest sensitive information from infected Android devices that attackers could use to gain access to victims' cryptocurrency accounts.

In contrast, the newer versions that Zimperium is tracking pack considerably more capabilities. These include remote device control and surveillance, credential and keystroke theft, screen capture, live screen streaming, microphone monitoring, and the theft of SMS messages, contacts, and call logs. Another feature allows attackers to steal or change device lock-screen credentials, potentially locking victims out of their devices.

Since July, Zimperium analysts have identified 78 unique malware samples, 42 dropper samples, 36 payloads, and 21 IP addresses that the malware operators have been using for command-and-control communications. The researchers also identified 129 distinct commands that attackers can use to remotely control infected devices, steal information, monitor user activity, and manipulate device functions.

Related:Indonesia Hit by Android Banking App-Cloning Campaign

The operators of ArcticRAT 2.0 are using malvertising, smishing, and third-party forums to direct visitors to malicious websites in which the malware is embedded, "The primary attack vector," according to Zimperium, "relied on a landing page that convincingly impersonated Google Play to trick targets into downloading a malicious application." In some instances, the researchers observed the attackers using Amazon Web Services storage buckets to deliver the payload directly on Android devices.

Once installed, the latest version of ArcticRAT — like prior versions — abuses Android Accessibility Services permissions to connect with its command-and-control (C2) servers, giving attackers remote control over the device. The malware first collects information about the compromised device, including its location, battery status, screen state, Wi-Fi connectivity, and currently active applications.

It sends the information to the cyberattackers, who can then select which functions to activate based on the victim's device and installed applications. This can include actions as varied as capturing keystrokes, taking screenshots, recording screen activity, monitoring microphone audio and extracting sensitive information from messages and applications.

Related:ToxicPanda Banking Trojan Matures Into Enterprise Threat

One of the more significant additions to ArcticRAT is its use of artificial intelligence to analyze information stolen from compromised devices and identify data of potential financial value. Zimperium found the malware featuring an API connection to xAI's Grok model, which attackers can activate remotely to examine the victim's installed applications and identify banking, cryptocurrency, and trading platforms.

The new AI capabilities allow ArcticRAT to process stolen SMS messages, separate routine communications and promotional messages from information such as one-time authentication codes, account balance changes, and transaction notifications. It can even estimate a victim's financial standing before sending the information to its command-and-control infrastructure, according to Zimperium.

This allows attackers to automate much of the work involved in sorting through large volumes of stolen information and identifying potentially valuable financial intelligence, rather than having to manually examine the data themselves, according to the firm. "As mobile Trojan threats like ArcticRAT become increasingly sophisticated, conventional signature-based security layers are no longer sufficient to protect enterprise mobile endpoints."

ArcticRAT's transformation from a targeted cryptocurrency stealer into a sophisticated RAT is an example of how quickly mobile threats are evolving, with attackers using AI to make their malware more capable and dangerous. Analysts have noted how the trend underscores the need for users and organizations to stop treating their mobile devices as secondary security concerns and instead apply the same level of threat monitoring, access controls and security protections as they do to traditional endpoints.

#9708. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

#9707. China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

Attackers used Cairn once again in autonomous attacks that targeted advanced manufacturing and defense sectors, as well as civil and human rights organizations.

China-nexus threat actors unleashed another wave of attacks using autonomous AI tools to compromise microprocessor manufacturers, US defense contractors, and other organizations.

The malicious activity, tracked as CL-STA-1238 by researchers at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42, is the second documented attack in which China-linked actors used the open source AI penetration-testing framework called Cairn for automation, they revealed in a blog post. In this latest campaign, attackers conducted 25 operations between August and September against at least 19 organizations, achieving "unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of the targeted organizations," according to the post.

In the successful attacks, the threat actors obtained dozens of valid credentials; achieved mass exposure of personal data, exceeding 1 million records at one organization; retrieved military and government identities; created persistent administrator accounts in a production system; and modified a live industry standards-ballot document.

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

Of the total organizations targeted, seven were in the semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain, and three organizations were in US defense and defense policy. The attackers also targeted various human rights and civil society organizations.

According to Unit 42 researchers, the victims included a industry standards body, which suffered a password-spraying attack; a semiconductor company, where attackers brute-forced a production credential on a partner-integration application; a US teacher's union, which suffered an unauthenticated account-creation bypass on a content management system; and a defense policy think tank, where attackers targeted an open back-end registration endpoint on its identity platform.

The China-nexus actors also targeted content management systems through identity and configuration weaknesses at other organizations, including a semiconductor-lithography manufacturer, an industrial-automation manufacturer, and an education nonprofit.

Cairn played a significant hand in the campaign, and the use of it "represents a shift in how attackers are applying AI to targeted offensive operations," according to the post.

"The attackers supplied a target and a goal, then Cairn planned, executed, and recorded results on its own," Unit 42 researchers wrote.

Cairn is AI model agnostic, and in this case, attackers weaponized it using Chinese large language models (LLMs) Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash and Pro. However, initial exposure to the organizations' networks came through many of the traditional security gaps found across industries, the researchers noted.

Related:Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

"It doesn't matter much to a victim whether a human or an AI agent is behind the keyboard," Tyler Oliver, CEO and founder of threat-hunting platform Huntbase, tells Dark Reading. "A human might hand the tool a mission and walk away, or direct it step by step. Either way, the password spraying looks like password spraying."

Indeed, the vulnerabilities the attackers exploited were known, according to Unit 42, including "authentication bypasses; insecure direct object references; mass-assignment privilege escalation; weak and default credentials; exposed cloud APIs; and dated public CVEs."

As in the previous Cairn-driven attacks, the findings once again provide a look under the hood about how threat actors can weaponize the tool against organizations, a blueprint that may be used in future attacks.

Rather than manually directing every stage of an attack, operators supplied Cairn with a target and a high-level objective. The framework then developed its own plan, conducted reconnaissance, identified potential vulnerabilities, attempted exploitation and recorded its findings.

Related:CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

"An AI model drives each Cairn 'agent worker,'" according to the post. "Cairn coordinates its activities through a shared 'blackboard.' Agents read the blackboard and write their findings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject 'hints' at any time to help guide the operations if needed."

"Cairn has a shared record of what it's already learned, so it can build on earlier findings without a person reviewing every result and deciding what happens next," Rickard Carlsson, CEO of AI security firm Detectify, tells Dark Reading. Meanwhile, this ability to work with limited supervision is already showing up across multiple tools including another AI penetration-testing framework, Artex, which also is being weaponized by attacker, he says.

Individual CL-STA-1238 operations lasted anywhere from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, according to Unit 42. Moreover, attackers could achieve simultaneous operations against multiple organizations, which reduced the dependence on human operators to manage each intrusion.

Though AI is changing the game in terms of speed, volume, and expanse of attacks, it does not change the "complexity" of attacks, which, as mentioned, often rely on known security gaps, according to Unit 42.

That's a spot of good news for defenders, because "identity hygiene, attack-surface reduction, and software patching remain effective" against attacks that use Cairn or other AI tools, according to the post.

However, there are other safeguards that organizations can put in place to defend against AI-driven attacks, too, says John Strand, owner of security consulting firm Black Hills Information Security.

"There are two things I think every organization should be doing right now," he tells Dark Reading. "First, continuous attack surface management. Organizations need to identify all the different services and systems they have exposed to the internet and start restricting access wherever possible."

The second key defense move is to start using cyber deception as much as possible by setting up "tripwires" that can detect attackers during reconnaissance and lateral movement "before they accomplish their objectives," Strand adds.

Every sales team runs on a story about its customers. Who is the real decision-maker, what made the buyer pause on price, which rival came up on the last call and what the team promised to send by Friday. For 25 years, the software meant to hold that story has asked salespeople to type it in by hand. Most of the time, they don't.

That gap sits inside one of the largest markets in business software. Salesforce earned $21.6 billion of CRM revenue in 2024, a 20.7% share that implies a global customer relationship management (CRM) market of about $104 billion (our arithmetic), while the category grew 12.8% in a single year. Yet salespeople still spend only 40% of their time selling, losing the rest to research, admin and data entry that their systems were supposed to remove.

Dreamteam is built on a different design, one where the CRM listens and acts without waiting to be told. The AI-native CRM, founded in 2025 by three former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million across its Seed and Series A rounds in a round led by Accel, with participation from Premji Invest and from Together Fund, the company's first institutional investor and seed lead. Hundreds of companies already use it, including teams at Plex, invideo and Lookout.ai.

Salesforce has led CRM revenue for 12 straight years, with Microsoft its nearest rival at $5.45 billion, while Adobe, Oracle, SAP and HubSpot divide much of what remains. The market is far from saturated. It grew 12.8% in 2024, faster than Salesforce's own 9.5%, which nudged the leader's share down from 21.7% to 20.7% as spending spread across more vendors.

What has barely changed is the design. Legacy CRMs were built around structured fields and hand-coded workflows, which record a deal stage or a contract value well. They struggle with the signals that actually decide deals, such as a prospect who sounds unsure, a board that has started questioning costs or a competitor named in passing on a call. Every new tool a company adds to fill that gap scatters the customer story across one more system.

Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of 4,050 sales professionals found that sellers spend 40% of their time selling. The other 60% goes to research, data entry, admin and internal work. Nearly half of sellers say they lack the bandwidth for proper outreach, even though prospecting already eats close to a full workday each week.

Sales teams have already chosen their fix. 87% of sales organizations use AI in some form, while sellers expect prospect research time to fall 34% and email drafting time to fall 36% once AI is fully in place. The obstacle is data. 51% of sales leaders using AI say disconnected systems are slowing their projects, which is exactly the gap an AI-native CRM is designed to close.

AI agents, software that can carry out tasks on a person's behalf, are moving from pilots into daily sales work. 54% of sellers have already used one, 55% use AI for prospecting and nearly nine in ten plan to use agents by 2027. The best teams are moving first, as top performers are 1.7 times more likely than underperformers to use prospecting agents.

An agent is only as good as what it can see. 79% of high performers prioritize data hygiene, compared with 54% of underperformers, while 74% of sales professionals say they are focused on cleaning their data. A CRM that captures context automatically hands every agent a complete, current view of each customer without that clean-up work.

Dreamteam's $53 million spans its Seed and Series A rounds. Accel led the funding, while Premji Invest and Together Fund participated. Together Fund, founded by Freshworks co-founder Girish Mathrubootham, led the seed round and was Dreamteam's first institutional investor, which means the founders' former colleague backed them from the first day.

The raise puts Dreamteam among the best-funded AI-native CRM startups so far. Attio raised a $52 million Series B in August 2025 led by GV, while Day AI raised a $20 million Series A in February 2026 led by Sequoia, so Dreamteam's total is about 2.7 times Day AI's round (our arithmetic). The pattern is clear: investors are funding a new generation of CRMs designed for AI from the first line of code, not legacy systems with AI added on top.

Dreamteam starts by listening. It connects to a team's email, calendar, meetings and other tools, then builds what it calls the Company Brain, a living memory of the business. From every interaction it pulls out the signals that matter, including buyer intent, objections and price hesitation, competitor mentions, stakeholder dynamics and the commitments each side made. The CRM updates itself, so salespeople no longer have to.

Four specialized AI teammates then put that memory to work. Rachel, the research assistant, enriches every account and contact. Sally, the sales assistant, prepares for meetings, drafts follow-up emails and manages tasks. Raj, the RevOps partner, watches the pipeline, flags deals at risk and sharpens forecasts, while Alex, the CRM administrator, sets up and runs the system in plain language.

People stay in charge of the result. Sales teams review and approve the actions their AI teammates propose, while sales leaders can ask questions that legacy CRMs struggle to answer, such as which deals are stalling and why. Each teammate arrives trained for its job, so companies do not have to build and train their own agents before they see value.

Dreamteam is also built to work with other AI. It offers a first-class API and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, the open standard that lets AI assistants connect to outside software, so teams can work with their CRM from tools such as Claude. Its Magic Apps feature brings vibe coding, building software by describing it in plain language, into the CRM, letting business users create custom apps and dashboards without writing code.

Dreamteam built its product alongside a small group of fast-growing, AI-forward sales teams, which kept it anchored in real sales workflows from day one. Today hundreds of companies use it across AI, online media, healthcare, manufacturing and consulting.

At invideo, the enterprise sales team began with a small pilot and soon rolled Dreamteam out to the whole team, with the CRM reviewing customer interactions each morning and surfacing insights the team had never been able to see. Plex co-founder Scott Olechowski has said the product hits the sweet spot between simplicity and powerful AI, singling out how well it works with existing AI tools such as Claude, while DMS Health chief executive Patrick Doyle believes it is far ahead of what other CRMs offer.

Dreamteam was founded by Anand Venkatraman, Ramesh Parthasarathy and Senthil Kanthaswamy, former senior executives at Freshworks who helped scale that company from its early startup days through its IPO. Each brings more than 25 years of experience building and selling B2B software. Between them, they have spent time at Microsoft, Salesforce, Akamai and Sun Microsystems.

They have also been building with AI longer than most. The founders shipped AI applications in the GPT-2 era and scaled them to tens of thousands of businesses, then watched traditional CRMs leave teams with stale pipelines and unreliable forecasts. When AI models learned to reason over context, they concluded the CRM could finally be rebuilt from the ground up. Dreamteam is headquartered in Sacramento, California.

Dreamteam's ambitions reach past the sales team. The company is building a shared intelligence layer across the full customer lifecycle, from the first conversation through customer success to upsells, while Magic Apps lets each business shape the CRM around how it actually works.

Every generation of CRM has been defined by a platform shift. Siebel rode on-premise software, Salesforce rode the cloud and Freshworks proved a new challenger could scale to IPO. AI is the next shift, while the market Dreamteam is chasing is worth more than $100 billion. With $53 million, hundreds of customers and founders who have already built one enterprise software company to IPO, Dreamteam is positioned to show what a CRM looks like when it does the work itself.

#9705. 'Sleeper Agent' Tactic Hides Payloads in Open-Weight AI Models

Malware can lurk inside just 0.00001% of a neural network. How, then, can any user tell it's there?

AI models downloaded from the open Internet can be subtly poisoned with malicious payloads if attackers are careful enough.

Open-weight AI models have become seriously popular lately. Even early last year, McKinsey found that 63% of organizations used them, and 76% of survey respondents said that they expected to use them more in the coming years. They're auditable, developers like using them, and, perhaps most of all, they're cheap.

Like any other software you can download off the Internet, however, open-weight and open source AI tools carry some degree of risk. Last week, researchers described a technique they call "Lazarus," which could allow an attacker to poison a model using a near-imperceptible few of its neurons. Microsoft described it as turning a model into a "sleeper agent," capable of granting an attacker access to its user's environment.

"A model is a file almost nobody inspects, yet we download models from strangers and give them access to our code, credentials, and systems," explains Briland Hitaj, senior AI security research engineer at Confidencial, whose research into techniques like this preceded Microsoft's. "Malicious models have already turned up on Hugging Face, though so far they abuse file formats like Python's Pickle to run code when loaded. I'm not aware of anyone hiding payloads inside the weights themselves outside research, but that's where the research points."

Related:Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

Since at least 2020, researchers have been coming up with clever ways to store bad stuff inside of neural networks.

The premise behind this whole category of research is that the size and complexity of these networks provide cover for small, secret, but potentially powerful payloads. Just look at Qwen 3.8-Max: It's totally open-weight, so you can inspect it to your heart's content. But it's made of 2.4 trillion parameters, and probably around 100 million neurons. If an attacker plants a functioning payload in some of those neurons or parameters, how exactly are you going to find it?

The trick, then, isn't finding a place to hide a payload. First, it's getting that payload to function reliably amid so many moving parts; second, it's making sure it doesn't noticeably impact the normal functioning of the model; and lastly, optionally making the payload robust to fine-tuning.

Different researchers have come up with different ways to do it. In 2022, Hitaj and his colleagues came up with a technique called "MaleficNet," which repurposed an old military and, later, 2G and 3G mobile network technique called "code division multiple access" (CDMA).

Related:November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs

Very simply, they split malware binaries into tiny pieces and spread the pieces across the many individual weights that make up a neural network. It wouldn't look like anything but noise to a passerby, yet with a trigger mechanism and a way to decode the weights, they could recover, recombine, and execute the binary.

"The vulnerability comes from how neural networks work, not from a bug," Hitaj explains. "Models have far more parameters than they strictly need, so you can nudge millions of weights slightly, or repurpose a few neurons that rarely fire, without visibly changing the model's behavior. And since nobody can read weights the way they read code, those changes go unnoticed."

Microsoft's new technique compromises on capacity for simplicity. Where Hitaj proposed encoding an entire binary across many model parameters, Microsoft researchers propose sneaking a brief command inside of fewer than 10 neurons. Specifically, one must target "dormant" neurons — those that prove to have little effect on the overall model's functioning — late in a model's processing cycle, and thus more directly influential over its output. One encodes a payload in these neurons, arranged to fire sequentially, and configures them to stay largely inactive unless they're fed a trigger. Eventually, you get a sleeper agent.

Related:OnlyFans Copyright Takedowns Expose Compromised Websites

The target payload can be arbitrary, so long as it's small and formatted correctly. The trigger can be any particular user input to the model, or tool output, or something so simple as a date read in a user's terminal.

Luigi Vincenzo Mancini, a professor at Sapienza University of Rome and one of the co-authors of the MaleficNet paper, advises organizations to take a defense-in-depth approach to open-weight AI security, "rather than trying to find a single magical 'AI malware scanner.'"

Like any third-party software, users should download AI models from official sources. As an added measure, users can compare the models they download with a known, trusted baseline.

"Microsoft says that reliable detection of these kinds of modifications requires being able to diff the deployed weights against the original, unmodified weights," Mancini notes. "That's a powerful argument for treating model weights more like source code or binaries than like ordinary data files."

Next, users should scan their models in general for anomalies. Though as Hitaj points out, "No scan proves a model is clean, and ordinary testing rarely finds a trigger the attacker chose. So the key controls limit what a compromised model can do: give AI agents only the access they need, keep credentials and production systems out of reach, restrict network access, log what agents do, and require human approval for consequential actions. If a model turns malicious, you want it boxed in and visible."

Beyond restricting them from the outset, "Organizations should monitor for unexpected agent behaviour at the system boundary," Mancini says. Practically speaking, "a model emitting an unusual shell command, attempting an unexpected network connection, accessing credentials it normally doesn't need, or suddenly invoking a tool in an unusual context can be a much more actionable detection technique than directly inferring malicious intent from billions of model parameters."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9704. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

#9703. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

#9701. Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, But Payments Decline

Large language models and other AI systems allow a growing number of ransomware groups to create convincing phishing emails and identify sensitive data quickly.

Ransomware attacks are expanding amid cybercriminals' increasing use of AI tools, but at the same time, fewer organizations are paying ransoms, according to multiple reports released this month.

Globally, organizations are seeing far more ransomware incidents, while the number of attacks targeting US companies has remained fairly steady. In the third quarter of 2026, for example, ransomware groups claimed 2,766 breaches, an increase of nearly 40% over the previous quarter, according to threat data released by cybersecurity services firm Halcyon.

Threat groups adopting AI is likely a major reason for the increase in attacks. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to create convincing social-engineering messaging, find sensitive data quickly, and assist attackers has largely driven the surge in attacks in other nations, says Cynthia Kaiser, senior vice president of Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center and a former deputy assistant director at the FBI's Cyber Division.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

"We think AI is a big part of [the growth] because it has removed the language barrier for phishing," she says. "We're now seeing much more convincing phishing in Japanese, for example. Countries like Japan are treating this almost as a state of emergency."

Overall, the jump in claimed ransomware cases — up 31% from Q1 and 39% from Q2, according to Halcyon's report — has not necessarily resulted in more ransoms paid out.

Take the retail sector as an example: While 62% of attacks on companies succeeded in encrypting data — up from 48% in 2025 — less than a third (32%) of retailers actually paid to get the data back, nearly half of the 58% that paid in 2025, according to Sophos's The State of Ransomware in Retail 2026 report.

Instead, a solid majority of retail firms (71%) recovered their data from backup, and most recovered within a week, Sophos found. Other sectors, such as local government and school districts, have seen declines in paying ransomware as well, says Chester Wisniewski, global field chief information security officer (CISO) at Sophos.

"None of them are paying the ransom," he says. "Whether there's extortion involved, whether data theft's involved, it kind of doesn't matter. They're largely not paying the ransom."

The number of ransomware groups claiming success took off in 2026, growing from 75 in Q1 to 111 in Q3, according to Halcyon data. While ransom amounts have continued to decline, the growth in the number of groups continues to pose a threat to companies, Sophos's Wisniewski says.

Related:Shadowy AI Relay Disables OpenAI Codex, Claude Code Sandboxes

"There's been five or six new names I've seen in just the last few weeks, so it doesn't seem like ransomware's going away at all," he says. "But its efficacy has been declining as far as generating actual money for the crooks."

The median ransom demand has dropped to $700,000 in 2026, from $2 million in 2024, according to Sophos data.

That hasn't stopped new ransomware groups from continuing to appear. At the end of the quarter, about a third of all claimed ransomware successes came from groups that didn’t exist six months earlier, says Duy-Phuc Pham, a malware researcher at Trellix.

"At the top, The Gentlemen grew from a few dozen victims a year ago to the most active group, ahead of Qilin," he says. "That kind of success makes them the obvious next target for law enforcement, which spent this year going after the shared services these groups depend on, from criminal VPNs to laundering services."

With attackers increasingly using AI, ransomware gangs will continue to broaden their campaigns against more industries in more regions — part of the reason that Europe has witnessed an increase in attacks, while US victims' share of incidents has remained the same or decreased, says Pham. AI allows attackers to create more convincing social-engineering messaging in a variety of languages, removing a significant historical barrier to targeting smaller populations.

Related:Researchers Infiltrate Microsoft Tech Support Scam Operation

Because of the greater scale that AI enables attackers to hit, ransomware threat actors are able to widen their coverage, he says.

"When a tool can scan, exploit, and move through networks with little human effort, a small crew can do the work of a large one, hit far more victims, and do it faster," Pham says. "That fits what we see on the leak sites: more groups and more newcomers."

The manufacturing sector continues to be the top target of ransomware gang, because suppliers and partners often share the same platforms, so a single compromise can expose engineering data beyond the targeted company, says Halcyon's Kaiser.

The sector will likely continue to be the top targeted group in 2027, especially as international organizations continue to account for a greater share in the coming year, she says.

"I'd expect continued growth, especially outside the US," Kaiser says. "The big open question is whether more attacks means more money ... countries newly feeling the pain are paying much more attention, which should improve international cooperation."

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. #9699. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

This entry was posted on Wednesday 4th of November 2026 11:36 PM

One useful technical distinction is that AS2650 is an autonomous system, not a single subnet. For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. That matters when a residential proxy makes traffic look trusted simply because the address falls inside an organization’s announced space. I maintain OnlinTools; our Subnet Calculator can show the network, range, broadcast address and host count for a supplied CIDR prefix, but it cannot establish route origin, physical location, ownership, or compromise.

Interesting how a seemingly ordinary device can turn a trusted network into an access point for someone else’s traffic.

What makes this particularly concerning is that the organization may remain completely unaware of how its own infrastructure is being used. A good reminder that information security also depends on visibility into what is actually happening within a network.

The location detail is what separates this from ordinary proxy noise: AS2650 is a fixed, well-known allocation, so any exit node registered there is either a misconfiguration worth escalating internally or an actual beacon worth watching – there’s no third reading. That Infatica nodes bundled into free apps are the vector fits the broader pattern where the resource being rented out belongs to someone who never knowingly agreed to rent it. The persistent two-week window suggests nobody at the network’s edge was watching egress, which is the cheap fix here.
